entry.title: Naruto
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Twelve years after a nine-tailed fox spirit attacked the Village Hidden in the Leaves and killed its leader, the Hokage, a troublemaking orphan named Naruto struggles to graduate from the ninja academy while dreaming of becoming Hokage himself (VIZ blurb via AniList and MU). The long series follows his training, team bonds, rivalries and wars, with revenge, betrayal and friends turning into enemies as recurring threads (MU and AniList tags; Bark review).
entry.life_message: Perseverance, friendship and refusing to give up on people can turn an outcast into someone who protects his whole community.

content.note: Frequent weapon and technique fights without explicit gore (Bark); War, Revenge, Martial Arts (AniList); deaths of family members (MU).
Tragic pasts, orphans, war and necromancy (AniList Tragedy 78, War 83, Necromancy 70); Bark suggests previewing intense scenes.
Romance hinted, no explicit scenes (Bark); love triangle (AniList); any gag fan service not checked (to verify).
Rare mild language (Bark).
None noted in sources opened (to verify).
Isolation of an orphan, tragic pasts and 'inner demons' (MU Tragic Past, Inner Demon/s, Dead Family Member/s).
Ninja weapons and fighting techniques throughout (Bark; AniList Ninja) (to verify).
Large multimedia franchise with games and films (MU Adapted to Game, Movie).

entry.dominant: Found family and village loyalty; perseverance virtue; cycles of revenge explored

frames.aligns: Naruto's refusal to abandon friends mirrors charity; dignity of the outcast orphan.
frames.concerns: Spirit-fox power and necromancy; ninja killing normalized.

frames.aligns: Humility and perseverance of a rejected child.
frames.concerns: A demon-fox sealed inside the hero; summoned dead; war as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, hard work and second chances for rivals; clean language (Bark).
frames.concerns: Fox spirit, summoning and necromancy-like techniques.

frames.aligns: Redemption arc for an outcast; strong friendship ethic.
frames.concerns: Chakra and spirit powers read by some as occult.
Demonic fox sealed in a child, summoning and raising the dead.

frames.aligns: Duty to community and lawful leaders; common-grace virtues.
frames.concerns: Revenge cycles and magic powers framed as heroic.

frames.aligns: Vocation-like devotion to one's role in the village.
Mercy toward enemies and social belonging for the excluded.
A coming-of-age epic with clear good and evil framing.
frames.concerns: Length and violence of war arcs.
Ninja soldiers and war shown as heroic vocation.

frames.aligns: Inclusion of an ostracized child; peace through understanding.
Patience, loyalty and protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Spirit-beasts and necromancy like sihr; reviving the dead.

frames.aligns: Dharma of a protector; teacher-student devotion like guru bonds.
Breaking cycles of hatred is a stated theme (AniList Philosophy, Revenge).
Empathy and self-made effort over fate.
Loyalty, duty to village and respect for teachers and leaders.

frames.concerns: Spirits of the dead revived and fought with; fox spirit possession.
Spiritism, demon fox, violence and war central.

frames.aligns: Belief in oneself overcomes fear and limitation.
Worth of every person, even the feared outsider.
Nature spirits and animal summons treated with respect.
Fox spirit and kami-like beasts familiar; village harmony.
Courage defending one's people; overcoming ego through service.
Unity across divided nations as a goal (AniList War, Philosophy).

frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for the group over self.
Necromancy and sorcery; time spent on entertainment.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge and personal rivalry drive key characters (AniList Revenge 92; MU Friends Become Enemies).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Ninja academy, ranks and missions structure life in the village (VIZ blurb; MU Training).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to the whole village and to a found family of teammates (AniList Found Family; MU Teamwork).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hokage as village leader is the hero's goal; teachers and ranks respected (VIZ blurb).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Inherited ninja ways and spirit beasts shape the world (AniList Ninja, Necromancy).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Wars and threats to the village keep security central (AniList War).

folkways.japan: Teacher-student bonds, rank within the village and duty to the group echo Japanese senpai-kohai and workplace norms, framed through a folkloric fox spirit.

delivery.evidence: Bark lists friendship and perseverance as the themes carried by the story; no source on speeches (to verify).

personified.ideology: Never give up; bond with and redeem others

delivery.note: The message of perseverance and friendship is carried by the hero's arc; how villains' views on revenge are handled needs a full read (to verify).

entry.winners_losers: Naruto and his friends win through persistence and bonds; those driven solely by revenge or hatred are the main losers. Sympathy goes to community loyalty and second chances.

entry.heading: Hell's Paradise: Jigokuraku
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is an ordinary, chosen one: love that gives you a reason to live, honest bonds formed across enemy lines, and balance instead of extremes. Immortality bought by harvesting others, and obedience that empties out the self, are what the story rejects.

content.framing: Mixed: fan service neutral; coerced sex condemned

frames.aligns: Self-made "gods" seeking eternal life by consuming others are exposed and fall; faithful marriage as the reason to live; mercy and conversion of hardened killers; the dignity of the condemned.
frames.concerns: Sex shown as a power technique and coerced sex depicted (CCC 2354 on pornography); Taoist energy treated as real; explicit nudity. Inter Mirifica 7: evil may be shown if not made attractive, so the manga's fan service is the sticking point more than the gore.

frames.aligns: Rejection of false gods and self-deification by theft; repentance-like change in Gabimaru; love stronger than death.
frames.concerns: Theosis is the true "becoming divine," so the Tensen's self-made divinity by sex and harvesting can read as its dark parody, but Taoist cultivation is still shown as real power. Nepsis makes the nudity and gore a strong concern.

frames.aligns: Idols exposed as frauds; faithful husband; sinners changed by love.
frames.concerns: Taoist cosmology and sex magic shown as real; nudity and sex scenes fail many families' Philippians 4:8 test. Each congregation and family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; false religion and self-salvation fail; a hardened killer learns love; grace-like second chances for convicts.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian metaphysics is the world's working system; sexual content in the manga; no source of salvation beyond human bonds.

frames.aligns: Clear exposure of false gods and their cruelty; love and courage.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": Taoist energy work, sex magic, deity-faced monsters and chanting tree-people are central and shown as real power; the heroes win by mastering that energy. Views range widely.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed in the island's "paradise" that is really hell; idolatry exposed; common grace lets families value the craft and the critique.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment, which applies to the manga's nudity and sex scenes.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: no one saves themselves; the Tensen's self-salvation project collapses. Vocation: the executioner's office and its burden of conscience.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; Taoist metaphysics shown as real. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Transformation of hardened characters; works of mercy toward outsiders (Nurugai); holiness of marriage.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules ask to avoid diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; nudity and sex magic. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Good and evil judged by framing: false gods and predatory immortals condemned; love and mercy win.
frames.concerns: Fan service and sex magic; Taoist metaphysics. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on the gender themes.

frames.aligns: Capital punishment questioned; executioners who doubt killing; enemies reconciled.
frames.concerns: Violence remains the heroes' main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); conservative groups avoid such media entirely; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Marriage and family as the deepest good; reunion of husband and wife (ch. 127); service and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: nudity and sex scenes are unlikely to "invite the Spirit"; occult-style power.

frames.aligns: Critique of capital punishment, persecution of the Sanka and clan sexism; care for outsiders and children.
frames.concerns: Genderfluid beings cast as villains (Epicstream); sexual violence as plot material; fan service.

frames.aligns: Marriage fidelity; exposure of false religion and false promises of paradise.
frames.concerns: The tree-people's belief that souls go on to Hōrai, souls laid to rest, and spirit-like Tao conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; nudity and gore fail Fundamental Belief 22's standard.

frames.aligns: Exposure of false religion and those who pose as gods.
frames.concerns: Spiritism-like energy work and sex magic are central; violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality (Galatians 5:19-21) throughout.

frames.aligns: Love outlasts fear; false material "immortality" fails.
frames.concerns: Death, decay and bodily horror are shown as overwhelmingly real; the gore and body horror are exactly what members guard against.

frames.aligns: Idolatry exposed: beings who make themselves gods are destroyed; sanctity of marriage; doubt about executions echoes rabbinic reluctance on capital cases (Mishnah Makkot 1:10).
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the nudity and sex magic a strong concern; many Haredi homes would not have this book; human life harvested as "medicine."

frames.aligns: Critique of idolatry; sanctity of life and marriage; compassion for the stranger (Nurugai).
frames.concerns: Sexual content and coercion depicted; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Justice for the persecuted; questioning execution; tikkun olam echoes in protecting the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence and fan service; genderfluid villains.

frames.aligns: False gods (shirk) exposed and destroyed; only death is certain for all (Qur'an 3:185) and the quest for bodily immortality fails; faithful marriage.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the nudity and sex scenes a strong concern; deity images and Taoist power treated as real.

frames.aligns: Balance of opposites and energy (prana-like Tao) resonate; dharma of the warrior and of the householder; a faithful marriage; immortality-seeking demons in Puranic style end in ruin.
frames.concerns: Tantric-style sexual cultivation shown in a predatory light; tamasic gore (Gita 17).

frames.aligns: Craving for permanence (the Tensen, Rien's attachment to her dead husband) is the root of suffering; Sagiri's arc toward the Middle Way; impermanence accepted; nenbutsu chanted.
frames.concerns: Buddhist sacred names (Nyoirin Kannon and others) given to villains; deity-faced monsters; killing throughout, against the first precept; sacred chanting shown under false promises.

frames.aligns: Lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego shown in villains and condemned; courage to defend the weak; a faithful householder life.
frames.concerns: Sex magic and nudity; killing as the heroes' work.

frames.aligns: Unity across divisions (criminals and executioners); exposure of false gods; justice for the persecuted.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" against degrading art; constant violence.

frames.aligns: Respect for life, purity and sincerity (makoto) in Gabimaru and Sagiri; gratitude to those who sacrificed.
frames.concerns: Kegare (pollution): blood, death and decay saturate the island; the "paradise" is a site of impurity.

frames.aligns: Balance of opposites, plant and nature imagery, respect for the cycle of life and death; no stereotyping of witches.
frames.concerns: Nature and sexual energy shown mainly as tools of predators; "harm none" broken by the Tensen.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: be faithful to your partner, do not murder, help children.
Critique of state killing, ethnic persecution and clan sexism; a capable female deuteragonist in a platonic partnership (ANN); a bisexual character treated casually (Kotaku).
frames.concerns: Gender-nonconforming beings cast as villains (Epicstream); coerced sex and a child-bodied victim as plot material; fan service; violence against women (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: People change through meeting others (Kaku's stated theme, Japanese Wikipedia); fraudulent religion exposed; meaning found in finite human bonds; compassion over rules.
frames.concerns: Gore and sexual coercion need context for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Marriage fidelity as the reason to live; courage and duty; family loyalty (the Aza brothers).
frames.concerns: Hierarchy, clan tradition and the samurai code are mostly shown as oppressive; nudity and sex magic; genderfluid beings. Some religious conservatives raise the occult framing.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of convicts, outsiders and the persecuted; free search for truth (Senta's study of religions); critique of execution.
frames.concerns: Gender-nonconforming villains; sexual violence; graphic content for age.

frames.aligns: Exposure of false gods and invented religion; the individual's will to live a chosen life against village and state; skepticism.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Mei) is condemned in the story, as in the Eleven Rules; the Tensen's harvest of the weak.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The samurai and executioner code is questioned: Sagiri says "If abandoning such doubt is the way of the samurai then samurai I am not" (ch. 120). Mercy and the dignity of convicts outrank clan honor.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The village "hive mind," clan rules and the shogunate's order are shown as oppressive; Gabimaru wants a free, ordinary life (ch. 1).

Civic vs kin.evidence: A wife and brothers drive the plot (Gabimaru and Yui; the Aza brothers), but strangers and enemies form a lasting found family (Shion adopts Nurugai).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Convicts and executioners become equals; clan sexism (ch. 14) and persecution of the Sanka are critiqued.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Invented religion is exposed and Senta's study is a tool of reason, yet Taoist metaphysics is real in the world and Buddhist balance is valued.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Kaku calls it "a story of survival" (ANN 2025), but the goal of survival is a self-chosen, ordinary life of love.

folkways.japan: The Edo-period setting, the Yamada Asaemon executioner clan, ninja village loyalty and Buddhist and Taoist imagery are drawn from Japanese and Chinese history and lore (ANN 2026 feature). The story mostly critiques the rigid hierarchies of that setting rather than presenting them as its message.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness. Kotaku notes the violence is balanced by "humane compassion".
delivery.note: Themes of balance and humanity come through the Tao combat system and the convicts' and executioners' arcs.

personified.ideology: Doubt and compassion over rigid duty
Immortality and love turned to consuming attachment

lenses.lens: Taoist cosmology (added; not in the standard list)

entry.dominant: Taoist cosmology (added row), Existentialism, Secular humanism, Dharmic (Buddhist), Transhumanism (critiqued), Critical theory.

entry.heading: A Silent Voice (Koe no Katachi)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is possible even after doing serious harm: own what you did, make amends, learn to listen, and accept that your life still has worth. Despair isolates; communication and friendship heal.

content.frequency: Frequent in v1 and v6, occasional elsewhere

frames.aligns: Repentance, restitution and forgiveness (Formation Reimagined praises "the transformative power of giving and accepting true forgiveness"); dignity of a disabled person; evil shown but not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Suicide plan and attempt for younger or vulnerable readers (CCC 2280-2283 treats life as a gift; judgment left to God). Forgiveness comes without any reference to God.

frames.aligns: Repentance (metanoia) as a turning of the whole life; humility; love that bears another's burden.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) for the bullying and despair scenes; no sacred dimension to the healing.

frames.aligns: Clear wrong and consequences; confession and restitution (Luke 19:8, Zacchaeus); kindness to the weak.
frames.concerns: Suicide content and some coarse language measured by Philippians 4:8; redemption has no Christian source. Each congregation and family decides.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; strong grace and redemption echoes (Beneath the Tangles: worth is not measured by deeds).
No occult or spirit content; repentance and restored relationships.
frames.concerns: Despair and suicidal thinking as spiritual as well as emotional battles; language.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: every classmate, not only the lead bully, is shown complicit. Common grace allows valuing a non-Christian work.
frames.concerns: Suicide (WLC Q136 on self-murder, handled pastorally) for vulnerable readers; moral repair without God.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: Shoya cannot undo what he did; forgiveness comes from others. Entertainment as adiaphora, judged by love.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy and restitution; growth in character; care for the excluded.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: wrongdoing is named and repaired; reconciliation among a community.
Confession and reconciliation within a community; nonviolent repair of harm; restorative rather than punitive justice.
frames.concerns: Separation from popular media in conservative groups; violence and coarse speech in the bullying. MC USA families more open.

frames.aligns: Repentance and restitution; family sacrifice; worth of every soul.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; coarse language. For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Inclusion of a disabled person; critique of an excluding system; confession and repair.
frames.concerns: Critics' point that the deaf girl's voice is secondary to the bully's arc (Thunderword).

frames.aligns: Restored relationships, care for the vulnerable, self-worth; no spirits or occult.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" applied to the bullying and despair scenes; Fundamental Belief 22.

frames.aligns: No spiritism or occult; forgiveness and peace-making.
frames.concerns: Violence (Psalm 11:5) and bad language in the bullying; a romance with a former tormentor. Choices left to conscience.

frames.aligns: Love overcomes fear and hatred; healing of relationships.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on despair, injury and coma ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Teshuvah (repentance): recognizing the wrong, regret, asking forgiveness and restitution, as Maimonides describes; human dignity (kevod ha-briyot).
frames.concerns: Suicide traditionally grave; lashon hara and cruel speech on the page; many Haredi homes restrict secular media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; dignity of persons with disabilities; care for life.
Tawbah (repentance), seeking forgiveness from the person wronged, patience (sabr), mercy; mocking others is condemned (Qur'an 49:11).
frames.concerns: Suicide forbidden (Qur'an 4:29), here shown as an attempt that fails and is not endorsed; coarse language; a kiss on an unconscious boy.

frames.aligns: Karma and its fruits; making amends; ahimsa toward the weak; duty to family.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond the suicide themes.

frames.aligns: Right speech and its absence; karma and remorse; compassion (karuna); suffering arising from isolation and craving for approval.
frames.concerns: Right-speech concern with the cruel language on the page.

frames.aligns: Service and humility; anger and ego (two of the five vices) shown in the bullies and overcome.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond the suicide themes.

frames.aligns: Unity, consultation, kindness to the disabled; service through the group project.
Sincerity (makoto) in Shoya's apology; harmony restored within a community; coming-of-age rite (ch. 62).
frames.concerns: Little religious content to align or conflict.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" and the consequences of harm; healing of community.
The Way to Happiness precepts: be worthy of trust, do not harm a person of good will, help others.
frames.concerns: Despair handled through friends and family rather than any method the Church endorses; no psychiatry shown (to verify).

frames.aligns: Anti-bullying, disability inclusion, sign language, systemic failure of the school (Kaminishi).
frames.concerns: Deaf girl centered on a hearing bully's redemption; Shoko apologizes to the person hurting her (Thunderword); romance with a former tormentor; gendered expectations on Shoko (Weber). Safe-messaging concerns about suicide.

frames.aligns: Human worth without earning it; empathy; responsibility; repair through reason and relationship.
frames.concerns: Suicide scenes need mental-health framing; neither suicidal character gets professional help on the page (to verify).

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility, restitution, a mother's sacrifice, honest apology, character growth.
frames.concerns: Weak or absent adult authority; some coarse language.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person, including the one who did harm; justice for the excluded.
Compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2); harm to a child condemned; owning one's mistakes (Tenet 6).
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice and apology-centered ethics sit uneasily with Church of Satan individualism.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Insults and violence are not answered in kind; Ueno's attack on Shoko (ch. 44) and childhood fights are framed as wrong. Repair comes through apology and restitution, not retaliation.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The school's rules and teachers fail to protect anyone (v1); the story does not call for stricter rules or for leaving people alone, but for people choosing to listen.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families sacrifice (mothers, Yuzuru), but the story's healing comes from a voluntary circle of classmates and the wider community (ch. 53-62).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teachers and parents are flawed; peers repair each other. Group harmony matters but rank does not.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religious answer; modern secular schooling and inclusion. The coming-of-age ceremony (ch. 62) is a cultural rite, not a faith claim.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-worth, expressing feelings and tolerance of difference are celebrated; Shoya's mother's hard work and the debt are respected but not the goal.

folkways.japan: Formal apologies between families, group harmony, the fear of standing out, school-class social dynamics and the coming-of-age ceremony (Seijin no Hi) are Japanese norms the story uses as its setting; its critique of how Japanese schools handle bullying and disability was taken up by Japanese public bodies.

delivery.evidence: SLJ calls its bullying portrait "so balanced that I not only understood why people bully"; Thunderword says the deaf girl lacks agency.
delivery.note: The anti-bullying message is shown through each character's own point of view rather than stated by a narrator, with explicit apologies at key turns.

personified.ideology: Atonement is possible and a harmful person's life still has worth
The victim is to blame for the group's troubles

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Sakamoto Days
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a peaceful, ordinary family life. Even a killer can start over, and he makes up for the lives he took by protecting and helping others, never by taking more.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (killing condemned; non-lethal force endorsed)

frames.aligns: Conversion of life through married love; restitution by service (Aoi's demand that he help others to make up for past killings); sanctity of life; mercy to a defeated enemy; evil not made attractive in the villain (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Allies who still kill are glamorized; weight mockery against human dignity; language.

frames.aligns: Repentance (metanoia) as a turned life; the family as a "little church" of peace; mercy over vengeance.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (guarding the senses) makes constant combat and swearing a concern for stricter families.

frames.aligns: A changed life; a faithful husband and father; protecting children; justice left to lawful authority (Romans 13) at the end.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the gore and profanity; no gospel source for the change. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts violence without endorsing killing; redemption and second chances; marriage as a transforming covenant.
frames.concerns: Romans 14 conscience on violent entertainment; crude language; fat jokes.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; family protection; a changed life.
frames.concerns: Psychic mind-reading (Shin) as a normal power; worldliness of the assassin setting. Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a non-Christian work; the sixth commandment (WLC Q135-136) on preserving life shown positively; lawful judgment of Uzuki.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139-style caution on coarse speech; change grounded in human love alone.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: Sakamoto leaves final judgment of Uzuki to lawful authority (ch. 282-283); vocation as husband, father and shopkeeper.
frames.concerns: Entertainment as adiaphora, but LCMS and WELS families may weigh the language and violence more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; sanctification as a changed way of life; social concern for orphans exploited as assassins.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches more cautious about crude language and violence than UMC.

frames.aligns: Framing of good and evil is clear; reform, forgiveness and lawful justice.
frames.concerns: Language and violence for younger readers. Episcopal and ACNA families differ little here.

frames.aligns: Refusal to kill is the hero's defining vow; enemy spared and treated (ch. 282); humble shopkeeping life.
frames.concerns: Force is still the hero's main tool and is shown as heroic and fun (Matthew 5:39); assassins as cool. Closer to the tradition than most action manga, but on the dividing line. Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Family as central; a father who puts family first; repentance and restitution; children protected.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: language and constant violence may not "invite the Spirit." Members vary.

frames.aligns: Redemption, mercy, critique of an institution that exploits orphans (Uzuki and Gaku).
frames.concerns: Weight-based mockery (Common Sense Media "fatphobia"); a mentally ill villain; mostly male lead cast.

frames.aligns: Life is sacred; family and Sabbath-like rest in ordinary life; temperance (Sakamoto discourages smoking).
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) applied to constant fighting and swearing; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Valuing life; family loyalty; a peaceful life chosen over a violent one.
frames.concerns: jw.org's question whether entertainment features what God hates, especially violence (Psalm 11:5): violence is the series' main content. Mind-reading may be read as spiritism by some. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love transforms a hardened man; harmony at home outlasts danger.
frames.concerns: Fear, violence and trauma dwelt on as real and powerful; "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh and the value of every life; teshuvah (return) of a former killer; shalom bayit (peace in the home).
frames.concerns: Nivul peh (coarse speech) in the anime; constant violence; many Haredi homes restrict such media. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; shalom bayit; sanctity of life; justice through courts.
frames.concerns: Language and weight mockery (ona'at devarim, hurtful speech). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in rebuilding a life; justice for exploited children; courts over revenge.
frames.concerns: Weight jokes and stereotypes; violence for younger readers. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Sanctity of life (Qur'an 5:32); tawbah (repentance) and making amends; protecting family; forgiveness preferred when able to punish.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and smoking shown casually; coarse speech; mocking others' bodies (Qur'an 49:11).

frames.aligns: Ahimsa as a vow; grihastha (householder) duty valued over the warrior's path; karma of past killing worked off through service.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore and swearing.

frames.aligns: The first precept (no killing) is the hero's rule; compassion to a defeated enemy; right livelihood: he leaves killing for a store.
frames.concerns: Fighting remains the plot's engine and is played for fun; what it feeds the mind (right mindfulness).

frames.aligns: The saint-soldier ideal: strength used only to protect; kirat karni (honest work) at the store; vices (anger, ego) shown in villains.
frames.concerns: Language and casual drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Service, family unity, transformation of character.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence: fighting, even non-lethal, is the heroes' path. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), gratitude and a harmonious household; purification of a "stained" life.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; blood as impurity in fights. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: "Harm none" echoed in the no-kill rule; no stereotyping of witches or pagans.
frames.concerns: Little to raise. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: "do not murder," care for family, help others.
frames.concerns: The villain's dissociative identity disorder is a psychiatric category; the series treats it as story device, not medicine. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Redemption; critique of an exploitative institution; courts over revenge; capable women fighters.
frames.concerns: "Fatphobia" (Common Sense Media) and weight jokes (ANN, The Manga Critic); a villain defined by dissociative identity disorder; the wife's role mostly domestic.

frames.aligns: Human life valued without religious grounding; people can change; reason and courts over vengeance; no pseudoscience presented as fact (powers are clearly fiction).
frames.concerns: Glamorized assassin culture for younger readers.

frames.aligns: A man gives up a dangerous career for marriage, fatherhood and a small business; protective fatherhood; loyalty; the wife's moral authority in the home respected.
frames.concerns: Language; violence for younger readers; distrust of institutions in a book without faith.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of the villain: Uzuki is spared and treated (ch. 282); justice and compassion for exploited orphans.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; weight jokes; portrayal of mental illness. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Self-reliance; distrust of a corrupt authority (the JAA); fierce protection of children (Eleven Rules); compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2).
frames.concerns: The hero binds himself to his wife's rule and a family-first ethic more than self-assertion; the story's ideal is quiet domestic life. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Old enemies seek revenge on Sakamoto, but he does not answer insult or attack with killing, and he leaves Uzuki's fate to a court (ch. 282-283). Weight insults are shrugged off.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The household runs by Aoi's rules, obeyed strictly, while the JAA's official order is corrupt and replaced (ch. 283).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family and the store's found family come first; every arc is triggered by threats to Hana, Aoi or the staff (ch. 32-54, 283).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Sakamoto is "boss," and the Order and JAA have rank, but rank-based authority is critiqued and the store staff are friends more than subordinates.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; a secular, practical outlook on life, with traditional marriage and family life.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Work, security and protecting a peaceful daily life are the highest goods; comedy and personal quirks are tolerated.

folkways.japan: The neighborhood store, a wife who manages the household and its rules, school-cohort loyalty (the JCC classmates) and bystanders who keep calm are Japanese everyday norms used as comic setting; the story's own message is the no-kill vow and family over glory.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media quotes "It's never too late to start over"; no review opened calls it preachy; reviewers focus on comedy and action.
delivery.note: The no-kill message is carried by a running household rule and by action choices more than by speeches.

personified.ideology: Strength restrained for family; no killing
Sanctity of life; atonement by service
Violent revenge on an abusive system

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism (family-first), Secular humanism, Traditionalism.

entry.heading: Dr. STONE
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent learning, building and sharing knowledge so that every person can live. Progress is slow, earned "ten billion percent" through work and cooperation, and it is passed down from parents to children.

frames.aligns: Faith and reason are not at odds in Catholic teaching, and the series honors reason, work and the dignity of every life (Senku revives everyone; the purge is condemned). Mercy to enemies; honor for a father (CCC 2214-2220). Evil is never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: A world with no God where science carries the hope of salvation; Equip.org warns science can become an idol. Revival nudity and the harem arc (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Love for parents and ancestors, memory of the dead (Senku at Byakuya's grave, ch. 45), mercy to enemies, humility in learning.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the nudity and harem panels a concern. The story's only "liturgy," the priestess's tales, is turned into data, which may feel like a flattening of the sacred.

frames.aligns: Hard work, honesty, compassion, rescuing the sick (ch. 40-43), clear wrong in Tsukasa's purge and Ibara's tyranny.
frames.concerns: No acknowledgment of God; humans save themselves. Philippians 4:8 applied to the nudity, harem and teens brewing alcohol. Each congregation decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Equip.org (Harrison Dulin) admires Senku's use of science "to help others" and says Christians can serve God as scientists. Beneath the Tangles sees "humanity and faith" in Senku's science. Depicts wrong without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Dulin: Senku "is not acting as a Christian," and science can demand "reverence and attention that belong to God." Fan service.

frames.aligns: Little occult content: "sorcery" and petrification are explained as science, not spirits (ch. 17-19, 227-231). Clear right and wrong.
frames.concerns: A wholly naturalist worldview with no spiritual realm; a priestess tradition demythologized. Modesty standards and the harem arc.

frames.aligns: Common grace: the series celebrates real knowledge of creation and cultural work (the cultural mandate, Genesis 1:28). Total depravity echoes in Ibara and in Tsukasa's view of corrupt adults.
frames.concerns: Humanity rebuilds itself with no reference to God's providence. WLC Q139 makes the harem and nudity panels a concern.

frames.aligns: Vocation: building, farming and healing as service to neighbor. The left-hand kingdom of reason and order is treated seriously; tyranny is resisted.
frames.concerns: No gospel and no God; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA about the fan service.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (healing Ruri, feeding the village), education for all, social holiness. Wesley valued science and medicine (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; holiness churches more cautious about nudity and alcohol.

frames.aligns: A tradition of science and faith together; good and evil framed clearly; mercy to enemies.
frames.concerns: The absence of God; fan service.

frames.aligns: Senku avoids killing, wins wars by bluff and invention (ch. 46-82), and forgives enemies; a mutual-aid village.
frames.concerns: Progress through technology is the story's goal, at odds with Old Order separation and plain living; violence still used. Conservative groups avoid most popular media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Learning and "the glory of God is intelligence" (D&C 93:36); family bonds across generations (Byakuya's records for his son); work and self-reliance.
frames.concerns: Revival nudity and the harem arc; teens brewing alcohol (Word of Wisdom).

frames.aligns: Science and faith compatible; care for the sick; rejection of eugenics and purges; justice for Ibara's subjects.
frames.concerns: Few women in leadership; "gorilla" jokes; harem arc.

frames.aligns: Health, education and medicine are valued in the tradition; nothing spiritist; the dead do not walk.
frames.concerns: Teens brewing and drinking alcohol; nudity; no Creator, and petrification explained by aliens. "By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18).

frames.aligns: Little violence or spiritism; love of family, honesty, hard work.
frames.concerns: The story's hope is a human-built "Kingdom of Science" that will fix the world, against the teaching that only God's Kingdom will. Alcohol use by teens; nudity.

frames.aligns: Goodness, cooperation and courage win; fear is overcome.
frames.concerns: The heroic turning point is a drug cure for disease (sulfa for Ruri's pneumonia, ch. 40-43); matter and material medicine are shown as the means of healing, against the teaching on spiritual healing.

frames.aligns: Love of learning, honoring parents (Exodus 20:12), preserving a tradition across generations (the Hundred Tales as a kind of oral law), saving life above all (pikuach nefesh).
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes the nudity and harem arc a concern; many Haredi homes restrict secular media; no God.

frames.aligns: Learning, saving life, honoring the dead and ancestors, tikkun olam echoed in rebuilding the world.
frames.concerns: Fan service applied through family modesty values.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy, education, tikkun olam, anti-eugenics; Boichi's Korean background and Japanese setting raise no stereotype concerns reported.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond fan service.

frames.aligns: Seeking knowledge ('ilm) is praised in the tradition; justice against tyrants; mercy; care for the sick.
frames.concerns: Teens brewing and drinking alcohol; revival nudity and the harem arc (Qur'an 24:30-31, lowering the gaze); creation and the end of the world explained with no reference to God.

frames.aligns: Knowledge (jnana) and duty (dharma) as paths; devotion to a teacher and father; ahimsa-leaning hero.
frames.concerns: A purely material account of the world; some families apply the Gita's sattvic test to the fan service.

frames.aligns: Compassion, patience, investigation of cause and effect; Senku avoids killing where he can.
frames.concerns: Progress and craving for more (Ryusui's openly stated greed) are celebrated; the eight-precept view of entertainment; intoxicants made and drunk.

frames.aligns: Honest work (kirat karni), sharing (vand chakna), service to all (seva); tyranny opposed; equality of all people versus Tsukasa's "pure" selection.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and fan service; ego in Senku and Ryusui (the five vices).

frames.aligns: Harmony of science and religion and the unity of humankind are core teachings; Senku's science is shared, serves everyone and rejects selective survival.
frames.concerns: Science shown without religion, which Bahá'í writings warn can drift into materialism; fan service.

frames.aligns: Gratitude to ancestors and founders, nature restored and beautiful (Boichi's untouched Japan), sincerity (makoto) in Senku's work; the village priestess is treated with respect.
frames.concerns: The priestess tradition is explained rather than kept as sacred; little else to raise.

frames.aligns: Respect for nature and lineage; "harm none" echoed in Senku's non-lethal tactics.
frames.concerns: "Sorcery" is unmasked as ignorance of science (ch. 17-19); Tsukasa's nature-first world is the villain's. No stereotyped witches.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: be industrious, be competent, safeguard and improve the environment, do not murder (Tsukasa's purge condemned).
frames.concerns: Gen Asagiri as a "mentalist" manipulator is a comic figure.

frames.aligns: Science, education and STEM; anti-eugenics and anti-authoritarian; Common Sense Media: "a lot" of positive messages (teamwork, scientific progress).
frames.concerns: Male-gaze art (SLJ); Ibara's harem used as plot; "gorilla" jokes; few women among the inventors; Anime Feminist's 2019 concern about female characters.

frames.aligns: Reason, evidence, cooperation and human dignity, with no supernatural; knowledge shared freely; religion's mysteries explained naturally but without contempt; free inquiry ("the more you understand about science, the more you realize there's so much you don't understand," Inagaki, VIZ).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; chemistry projects need safety talk.

frames.aligns: Respect for fathers, founders and inherited knowledge; earned authority; free trade and private initiative (Ryusui); utopian purges and tyrannies fail. One essay reads Senku as the conservative against Tsukasa's radicalism (Appuals).
frames.concerns: Progress framed as the highest good; village tradition superseded; fan service.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person (all 7 billion revived), free search for truth, democratic cooperation, justice against tyrants.

The Satanic Temple's tenet that beliefs should conform to the best scientific understanding fits Senku closely; skepticism of authority; rejection of tyranny; individual excellence (Church of Satan) in Senku and Ryusui.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; harm to the vulnerable (Ibara) condemned.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Senku answers insults with sarcasm, not vendetta; enemies are pardoned (Tsukasa, Hyoga, Xeno). Only Ibara's abuse is never forgiven. Worth comes from what you contribute.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Kingdom of Science runs on voluntary cooperation and trade; the rule-bound tyranny of Ibara (no new inventions, no leaving the island) is the counter-example (ch. 101-137).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin love drives key characters (Byakuya and Senku, Tsukasa and Mirai), but the goal is reviving all of humanity, strangers and enemies included.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senku leads and the village has a chief, but rank is earned by skill; elitism (Hyoga, Xeno) is defeated.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Sorcery becomes science (ch. 17-19); the priestess's tales become records (ch. 42-45); the petrifier is a machine (ch. 227-231).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival needs dominate the early story; later the joy of discovery, curiosity and personal passion ("This is exhilarating!") take center stage.

folkways.japan: The work ethic of steady effort, school-club-style teamwork, respect for teachers and the shonen ideal of friendship reflect Japanese norms; the secular, practical outlook also fits Japan's high secular-rational position on the World Values Survey map, so readers may see it as the setting's default more than an argument.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media lists "the value of scientific progress" as a theme; LessWrong calls Tsukasa "value-based opposition." No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The pro-science message is spoken openly in Senku's lines and Science Corner asides, while rival visions get a sympathetic hearing in Tsukasa and a thinner one in Ibara.

personified.ideology: "Pure youth" primitivism and purge of corrupt adults
Village priestess tradition and oral memory

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Naturalism, Pragmatism; Might makes right and Collectivism/authoritarianism are strongly critiqued.

entry.heading: Dorohedoro (Q Hayashida)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a shared meal, a loyal partner and a job you can keep. The world has no fair rulers, so you stick with your own people, keep your word to them, and laugh at the horror.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, hospitality and friendship; the abusive powerful (Chidaruma) are humbled; forgiveness between old enemies.
frames.concerns: Killing is rarely framed as wrong, so evil is often "made attractive" through comedy (Inter Mirifica 7); devils shown as benign or desirable; inverted crosses as decor (CCC 2115-2117 on the occult is about practice, but framing matters).

frames.aligns: Loyalty and shared meals; the proud devil ruler brought low (ch. 167).
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real, so friendly devils, devil exams and inverted crosses are a serious concern; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore a concern too.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, hard work, honesty among friends.
frames.concerns: Demons and Hell played as comedy and reward; occult imagery throughout (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); killing without consequence. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Friendship, sacrificial loyalty (Kaiman fights to bring back Nikaido, ch. 155), forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Many accept fantasy magic but are wary of demons and spirit dealings; here devils are rulers and role models. Depiction of sin is common but endorsement is the question.
Media as an "open door": devils and Hell are central, friendly and aspirational; heroes accept devil power (ch. 155); inverted crosses throughout. Views vary between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace: craft, humor and friendship by a non-Christian artist; depravity is everywhere and no one is innocent.
frames.concerns: Hell and devils made comic; WLC Q136 on killing applies to casual murder; nudity (WLC Q139).

frames.aligns: Daily vocation (cook, doctor, cleaner) honored; no character saves himself.
frames.concerns: Devils as benign rulers; occult throughout. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (Noi's healing, Vaux's free clinic, likely ch. 96 "Free Hospital"); hospitality.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions not done "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches more cautious than UMC; casual killing.

frames.aligns: Strong fantasy tradition judges by framing; friendship and loyalty.
frames.concerns: Good and evil are blurred: heroes kill freely and devils are not framed as evil.

frames.aligns: Simple work and shared meals; forgiveness of enemies at the end.
frames.concerns: Violence as fun and as the main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); occult setting. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.
For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; graphic violence, devils and nudity weigh against it; occult and spirit dealings avoided.

frames.aligns: Class critique (sorcerers exploit the poor); strong women not sexualized; casual acceptance of Turkey's gender (vol. 23).
frames.concerns: Glorified, comic violence; the poor's grudge becomes a mass-killing monster (ch. 148), so justice is mostly revenge.

frames.aligns: Friendship and work; the cruel ruler humbled.
frames.concerns: Spiritualism and revived dead; Hell as a living realm conflicts with teaching that the dead sleep; gore.
jw.org asks whether media features what God hates: violence (Psalm 11:5) and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21); both are central, and devils are friendly.

frames.aligns: Friendship and good humor outlast horror.
frames.concerns: Fear, gore and evil shown as powerful realities; "stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Hospitality, loyalty, honoring the dead (Fujita, ch. 167).
frames.concerns: Sorcery and necromancy (Deuteronomy 18:10-11) central; revived corpses; tzniut concerns with nudity; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Hospitality, loyalty, memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Sorcery forbidden but fantasy generally accepted; casual killing; revenge as motive.

frames.aligns: Class critique, women's strength, tolerance of difference.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; justice as mass revenge (ch. 148).

frames.aligns: Hospitality, loyalty, care for the injured.
frames.concerns: Sihr (sorcery) shown as normal and powerful; devils (shayatin) as rulers and role models; casual killing; nudity and lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Food and hospitality; a proud being humbled and reborn as a human baby (ch. 167).
frames.concerns: Black magic disapproved; much tamasic content (Gita ch. 17); violence without dharma.

frames.aligns: Impermanence and absurdity; devils' boredom as a picture of craving without end.
frames.concerns: Killing as comedy, against the first precept; little compassion for the killed.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, work, standing up to the oppressor.
frames.concerns: Magic rejected by the Gurus; anger and ego (two of the five vices) are often shown as fun.

frames.aligns: Friendship and unity across old enemies (ch. 166-167).
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; spiritualism discouraged; "chaste and holy life" counsel.

frames.aligns: Spirits and devils as part of a living world, like yokai; no disrespect toward kami or shrines; gratitude for food and work.
frames.concerns: Blood and death (kegare) everywhere; the grudge of the unburied dead becomes a monster, a familiar folk idea treated mostly as horror.

frames.aligns: Magic as part of the world, not shown as Satanic; respect for strangeness and bodies.
frames.concerns: "Harm none": sorcerers use magic to harm the weak, which may read as a negative picture of magic users; harm is rarely judged.
The Way to Happiness's "do not murder" sits against casual killing.

frames.aligns: Class critique; women not sexualized (Anime Feminist); casual acceptance of Turkey's gender; environmental decay.
frames.concerns: Glorified, comic violence; drug trade played lightly; Common Sense Media 17+.

frames.aligns: No supernatural moral authority; friendship, work and humor make life good; reason (Vaux, Kasukabe) is useful.
frames.concerns: Cruelty played for laughs; little moral reflection.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, hard work, small business, family-style bonds and keeping your word.
frames.concerns: Demonic and inverted-cross imagery; chaos without lawful order; gore.

frames.aligns: Worth of outsiders, women's strength, tolerance of difference.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; little justice beyond revenge.

frames.aligns: Devils and magic are not stereotyped as Satanic evil; self-reliance, loyalty, proportionate retaliation (Caiman's hunt); arbitrary power (Chidaruma) is punished.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; harm to the innocent (Ebisu, the Hole's victims) would be the concern.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are answered personally: Caiman hunts the sorcerer who cursed him (ch. 1 on); En's family avenges attacks on it; the Hole's dead take revenge as Hole-kun (ch. 148). There are no courts.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The lawless Hole and its free-for-all life are the norm; En's order is enforced by fear, not celebrated as law.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Partners and crews come first: Shin and Noi, Caiman and Nikaido, En's "family." Strangers are often fair game.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ranks are real (devils, En, his cleaners) and shown with affection, but the top devil is humbled (ch. 167) and humans and sorcerers mix at the Hungry Bug.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No sacred tradition guides life; Hell and magic are mechanics; science (Vaux, Kasukabe) and craft solve problems.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in a harsh world, but also food, parties, odd fashion and casual tolerance of difference (Turkey, vol. 23).

folkways.japan: The food culture (gyoza, the restaurant as home), oyabun-style crime "families," and the folk idea that the grudge of the unburied dead becomes a vengeful spirit are Japanese elements; the devils and inverted crosses borrow Western occult imagery as style rather than belief.

delivery.evidence: ANN's This Week in Anime calls it "a slapstick sitcom" in horror's skin; WSWS faults weak social analysis. No reviewer calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series gives sorcerers, humans and devils each sympathetic and cruel members, and states no message outright.

personified.ideology: Loyalty and finding yourself through friends
Power as amusement; nothing is serious
Grievance of the exploited turned to slaughter

entry.dominant: Pagan/occult (as setting), Absurdism, Communitarianism (found family), Might makes right (as the world's rule).

entry.heading: Uzumaki: Spiral into Horror
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story promotes no clear good life. It shows a universe that is indifferent to people, where obsession, fear and even escape all lead to the same end. What survives longest is loyalty between people who love each other, and the story does not say that loyalty wins.

frames.aligns: Evil is never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); loyal love between Kirie and Shuichi; U.S. Catholic finds value in its sense that reality "dwarfs human understanding."
frames.concerns: The ending invites despair, the opposite of the theological virtue of hope; self-mutilation and an obsession-death (ch. 1-2) read against CCC 2280-2283.

frames.aligns: Obsession as a picture of a passion that consumes a person (ch. 1, 6, 7).
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes sustained grotesque imagery itself a concern; no light, theosis or repentance anywhere.

frames.aligns: No sin is endorsed; family loyalty; consequences for obsession.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on most pages; the world has no providence or hope (Romans 8:28 contrasted). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts without endorsing; can be "engaged" as a portrait of a world without God.
frames.concerns: Despair as the final word; occult-like curse with no counter-power; grotesque imagery.
Media as an "open door": a supernatural curse that possesses minds and bodies and cannot be resisted is the content this tradition weighs most heavily.

frames.aligns: Common grace allows valuing skilled art by a non-Christian; the story's picture of a broken creation has a total-depravity echo.
frames.concerns: Blind fate replaces providence; no judgment or grace.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; the law-like inevitability of the curse can be discussed as "law without gospel."
frames.concerns: No gospel at all; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.
Wesley's rule on books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: A literary horror tradition (Lewis on myth, the gothic) judges by framing; nothing evil is glamorized; love persists to the end.
frames.concerns: Hopeless ending; self-harm scenes. Range across Episcopal and ACNA families.

frames.aligns: No heroic violence: the series never presents fighting as the answer. Humility before forces larger than oneself.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media (Schleitheim 4): conservative groups avoid it outright; despair and grotesque content. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family and loyal love; consequences for obsession.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit; the hopeless ending and grotesque content weigh against it.

frames.aligns: Attention to how the vulnerable suffer (children, the sick, the poor in the row houses); no scapegoating endorsed.
frames.concerns: Women and pregnancy shown as monstrous (ch. 10-11); no structural or communal answer offered.
"By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) applied to sustained horror; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment.
jw.org's question whether entertainment features what God hates: the supernatural curse leans toward the occult and violence (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Love outlasts much of the horror.
frames.concerns: The series presents fear, disease and bodily corruption as all-powerful and inescapable, the reverse of the teaching that they are unreal.
Despair over hope; self-mutilation (bal tashchit and preservation of the body); tzniut and the nudity; many Haredi homes avoid such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Nothing endorsed; family loyalty; a meditation on fear.
Informed autonomy; nothing stereotyped or antisemitic.
frames.concerns: Self-harm and despair need context for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Nothing evil is praised; human limits before forces beyond them.
frames.concerns: Despair of God's mercy is condemned (Qur'an 12:87), and the story ends in it; self-harm (Qur'an 4:29); lowering the gaze for the nudity; images of living beings debated.

frames.aligns: Cyclical time and repeated destruction echo cosmic cycles (yugas); obsession as a binding force.
frames.concerns: Tamasic (dark, fear-ridden) content under Gita 17; no dharma or release.

frames.aligns: Craving and aversion both bind: the father clings to spirals, the mother hates them, and both are destroyed (ch. 1-2); impermanence and cycles.
frames.concerns: What it feeds the mind (right mindfulness); no path out of suffering is shown.

frames.aligns: Attachment (moh) and ego shown as destructive (the hair rivalry, ch. 6; obsession, ch. 1, 7).
frames.concerns: Despair rather than chardi kala (rising spirits); self-harm.
The call to uplifting art and a "chaste and holy life"; the story offers no hope or service.

frames.aligns: A land under a curse (tatari-like) and the impurity of death and decay are familiar themes; old houses and places carry power.
frames.concerns: Kegare (impurity): the book dwells on corpses, blood and decay; no purification is possible.

frames.aligns: Nature's patterns (spirals, whirlwinds, snails) treated with awe; no stereotyping of witches or pagans.
frames.concerns: Nature shown as a hostile force rather than a sacred cycle.

frames.aligns: No psychiatry shown as a cure.
frames.concerns: Characters are helpless effects of a force beyond them, against the ideal of being "at cause."

frames.aligns: No harmful stereotype is endorsed; critics praise it as art; Common Sense Media notes the leads "seek independence and want to hold on to their individual identities."
frames.concerns: Pregnant women as monsters; Kirie's passive role; graphic self-harm (Common Sense Media 15+).

frames.aligns: Free inquiry: Shuichi studies the curse and is believed in the end; human bonds; supernatural horror read as fiction.
frames.concerns: Reason fails completely; no human answer works.

frames.aligns: Family loyalty and chaste romance; vanity and attention-seeking punished (ch. 6, 7).
frames.concerns: No virtue is rewarded; tradition (the old row houses, the ancient city) is a trap, not a refuge; despair over duty.

frames.aligns: Free search for meaning; dignity of each victim.
frames.concerns: Graphic content for age; no justice.

frames.aligns: No authority figure is trusted; individuals resist by their own will; horror as art valued.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No honor codes or vendettas; the family feud in ch. 5 is shown as part of the curse ("their souls have become twisted"), and the hair rivalry (ch. 6) is punished.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Neither order nor freedom saves anyone; the story celebrates neither.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Institutions collapse; what holds is the couple and Kirie's family, who protect each other to the end (ch. 13-19).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: No respected elders or ranks; adults are as helpless as teens.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Old row houses and the ancient spiral city are traps, but Shuichi's rational investigation fails too.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival is everything in the last volume; self-display (ch. 6, 7, "Galaxies") is punished.

folkways.japan: The nagaya row houses, small-town conformity, cremation customs and the inverted spiral of Japanese gag manga are Japanese settings and references (Wikipedia; Den of Geek). The fatalistic tone is the story's own, drawn from Lovecraft as much as from Japanese tradition.

delivery.evidence: Silverman (ANN): "we can feel the inevitability of the outcome." No review found calls it preachy; reviewers stress mood over message.
delivery.note: Every response to the spiral (obsession, fear, flight, resistance, surrender) is given a sympathetic hearing and the same fate, so no view is made a strawman.

entry.dominant: Nihilism (cosmic, not moral), Absurdism, Existentialism, Pagan/occult (folk curse).

series.title: Three Days of Happiness
series.romaji: Jumyou wo Kaitotte Moratta. Ichinen ni Tsuki, Ichimanen de.
series.native: 寿命を買い取ってもらった。一年につき、一万円で。

entry.heading: Three Days of Happiness (Jumyou wo Kaitotte Moratta. Ichinen ni Tsuki, Ichimanen de.)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A life's worth is not its market price, its length or its achievements, but how it is lived and whom it is spent caring for; even a short, failed life can end in real happiness through love and kindness. The story's ending (both leads give up their remaining time to share three last days) leaves open whether that is fulfilment or surrender, and readers split on it.

frames.aligns: Human worth is not market worth; despair gives way to love that serves another; Kusunoki pays another's debt. Evil (despair, revenge) is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Life is a gift held in trust, not owned or sold; trading it away, and the ending's choice of death, sit against CCC 2280-2283, though the story frames it as love. No hope beyond death is offered.

frames.aligns: Repentance from self-pity; humility; love that carries another's burden (Miyagi's debt).
frames.concerns: Despair (akedia) as a spiritual danger; life as God's gift; the ending's chosen death. Nepsis: what dwelling on hopelessness does to the soul.

frames.aligns: Worth is not earned by achievement; selfless love; honest confession of failure.
frames.concerns: Selling one's life and choosing death are treated as meaningful rather than sinful; no gospel hope. Philippians 4:8 test for a sustained hopeless mood. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Depicts despair without glamorizing it; a "lost" young man finds meaning in loving another; sacrifice for someone else.
frames.concerns: No God in the redemption; the ending can read as accepting death as the answer. Many families "engage" such stories to discuss them.

frames.aligns: No occult or demonic content; a supernatural shop treated as a plot device. Healing of a broken heart through love.
frames.concerns: Despair and suicidal thinking as spiritual as well as emotional battles; the deal with the shop as a picture of trading life away.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value a thoughtful non-Christian work; it exposes the emptiness of worth by achievement.
frames.concerns: Self-murder (WLC Q136) is the shadow over the premise and ending, handled pastorally; human life belongs to God's providence, not to a market.

frames.aligns: Worth received, not earned, has an echo: Kusunoki is loved before he changes. Entertainment as adiaphora, judged by love.
frames.concerns: The ending's chosen death; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Change of heart and works of mercy; growth in character over three months.
frames.concerns: Death by choice as the climax; holiness churches more cautious about a hopeless mood.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: the story critiques measuring life by money and moves toward love and gratitude.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent premise and ending for younger or vulnerable readers.

frames.aligns: Simplicity, contentment, service and self-giving over achievement.
frames.concerns: Separation from popular media in conservative groups; life laid down for a private romance rather than for faith or neighbor. MC USA families more open.

frames.aligns: Worth of every soul; repentance and change; service.
frames.concerns: Life is a probationary gift in the plan of salvation; selling it and choosing death conflict with that, though suicide is met with compassion (Handbook). For the Strength of Youth: does it invite the Spirit?

frames.aligns: Critique of valuing people by productivity; grace-like acceptance; care for the poor and indebted.
frames.concerns: Safe-messaging concerns; Himeno, a struggling young mother, gets little compassion from the plot (Harvard-hosted essay).

frames.aligns: Love and service change a life; no occult or spiritism.
frames.concerns: Death as a sleep and life as God's gift; "by beholding we become changed" applied to a sustained hopeless mood and chosen death.

frames.aligns: Kindness, honesty and caring for another; no spiritism reported beyond the unexplained shop.
frames.concerns: Life is sacred to Jehovah; trading it and choosing death; an unexplained supernatural power. Choices left to conscience.

frames.aligns: Love overcomes fear and despair; healing of a hopeless outlook.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on death, despair and a deadline to die ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Chesed (loving-kindness) and paying another's debt; the shop's verdict that a life is worthless is rejected.
frames.concerns: Life is of infinite worth and preserving it overrides almost every other command (pikuach nefesh); shortening it by choice, for money or for love, is grave. Many Haredi homes restrict secular media.

frames.aligns: Chesed, teshuvah from self-pity, care for the indebted.
frames.concerns: Sanctity of life; the ending's chosen death; safe-messaging for vulnerable teens.

frames.aligns: Critique of valuing people by productivity; tikkun olam on a small scale.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent ending; informed choice for families.

frames.aligns: Patience and kindness; rejection of the idea that a person is worthless; paying another's debt is praised.
frames.concerns: Life belongs to God and its term is His to set (ajal); taking or selling it is forbidden (Qur'an 4:29). The story treats giving up life as fulfilment. A romance outside marriage.

frames.aligns: Detachment from the fruits of action; karma-like reversal as kindness raises the worth of a life.
frames.concerns: Ending life early before its karma is worked out is discouraged; the story gives no sense of dharma beyond the couple.

frames.aligns: Impermanence and the present moment; suffering from craving for status and recognition; compassion (karuna) changes Kusunoki.
frames.concerns: Suicide is discouraged; the ending can read as attachment to one person rather than release. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: Ego (haumai) and self-pity overcome by service and love.
frames.concerns: Life is a precious gift; choosing death goes against hukam (accepting God's will).

frames.aligns: Service, kindness and the worth of every soul.
frames.concerns: Suicide forbidden; no spiritual frame for death.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in the late Kusunoki; gratitude for ordinary days; the seasonal, everyday beauty of a small town.
frames.concerns: Death as impurity is not a theme; little religious content to align or conflict.

frames.aligns: "Harm none"; the cycle of life and death accepted; love as a force for change.
frames.concerns: The ending's chosen death for younger readers.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be industrious, be worthy of trust.
frames.concerns: Hopelessness accepted rather than handled; life given up. No psychiatry shown (to verify).

frames.aligns: Critique of ranking people by productivity; youth poverty, isolation and a struggling young mother made visible.
frames.concerns: Safe-messaging guidelines: a suicide-adjacent premise with a death-by-choice ending, read by some reviewers as romanticizing "the easy way out" (MAL, Realhumanbean; novel reviewer Yorticus). Himeno's despair is not resolved. No help-seeking shown (to verify).

frames.aligns: Meaning made in this life through relationships and chosen values; worth not reducible to output.
frames.concerns: A chosen early death as the climax needs mental-health framing; no professional help shown (to verify).

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility, gratitude, keeping promises, paying debts.
frames.concerns: A young man trades away his future for a romance; family is estranged and absent; despair is never countered by duty, faith or community.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person, against the shop's pricing; compassion.
Satanic Temple: compassion and admitting mistakes (Tenets 1 and 6); bodily autonomy (Tenet 3) over one's own life.
frames.concerns: Church of Satan: self-preservation and living fully now; selling one's life cheaply and dying for another clashes with that individualism.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Slights are not answered in kind; Himeno's revenge plan is shown as despair, not justice (v2). Worth is inherent, against the shop's price.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The monitor system and its rules are coercive (Mangapedia); the story celebrates a person choosing how to spend his own time, within a framework he accepted.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is estranged and old friends hollow; the bond that matters is a chosen one with Miyagi; neither clan nor civic duty is celebrated.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The shop's ranking of lives is rejected; Kusunoki and Miyagi meet as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religious or customary answer; the question of worth is posed and answered in personal, secular terms.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Quality of life and happiness over length of life and security; art and love over money (v3).

folkways.japan: Young-adult isolation and the fear of being a burden, the weight of inherited family debt, the quiet small-town summer and festival setting, and a restrained, melancholy tone that some readers link to mono no aware are Japanese contexts the story uses; they are setting more than message (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers split: one says the ending is "a weirdly pessimistic way of shouting 'YOLO'"; another says it "reminds you" who you choose to be.
delivery.note: The theme of what a life is worth is stated openly through the appraisal and Miyagi's daily question, while the ending's meaning is left to the reader.

personified.ideology: A life's worth is measured by achievement and recognition, then by love given
Self-sacrifice and duty, paying for others at one's own cost
Despair and resentment turned into revenge
Lives can be priced by productivity and future happiness

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Utilitarianism (explored), Consumerism (critiqued).

series.title: Witch Hat Atelier
series.native: とんがり帽子のアトリエ

entry.heading: Witch Hat Atelier
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life uses one's skills carefully and creatively to help others. Power must come with responsibility, mistakes must be owned, and no one should be shut out of learning because of their birth or body.

frames.aligns: Responsibility, repentance for harm done, care for the weak, gifts used in service; evil (body-twisting magic, assault) is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Witches as heroes and spellcasting as a good (CCC 2115-2117 forbid real magic; fantasy magic is judged by its framing); a same-sex couple (CCC 2357-2359); the story's mixed view of authority.

frames.aligns: Watchfulness over one's power, humility, compassion for the suffering; the passions (pride, envy, despair) shown as harmful (Agott, Custas).
frames.concerns: Sorcery is strongly condemned in the tradition, and here "witch" is a heroic calling; body horror and mutilation feed fear; same-sex couple.

frames.aligns: Clear moral consequences, humility, kindness, confession of wrongdoing; no demons or spirit contact.
frames.concerns: Deuteronomy 18:10-12 forbids witchcraft, and the heroes are witches who cast spells; many Baptist families are cautious about spells even in fantasy (frame guide). Same-sex couple (BF&M 2000, XVIII). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Tolkien-style secondary-world magic with rules and limits; Plugged In: a "sweet show about a young girl who's striving to do good"; consequences for misuse; grace between rivals.
frames.concerns: Witchcraft vocabulary and playful spellcasting (Plugged In's main concern); same-sex couple (later volumes); the critique of authority.
Media as an "open door": witches as heroes, a pointed-hat witch culture, ritual sigils carved into bodies, magic as a positive path for children. Views range between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace: excellent art by a non-Christian; honest picture of human pride and the misuse of power (total depravity has an echo in good people like Qifrey doing wrong).
frames.concerns: Occult vocabulary; same-sex couple (conservative churches); WLC Q139 concern is low here (no fan service).

frames.aligns: Vocation: magic as a craft used to serve the neighbor; law and gospel echo in Coco's guilt and the mercy shown her.
frames.concerns: Occult vocabulary (Large Catechism, second commandment); LCMS and WELS families may weigh the witchcraft and same-sex couple more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy, holiness as love of neighbor, inclusion of the disabled and poor.
frames.concerns: Occult vocabulary; same-sex couple (Global Methodist, Wesleyan and Nazarene churches traditional; UMC affirming).

frames.aligns: A fantasy tradition close to Lewis and Tolkien (the creator names Tolkien as an influence, Wikipedia); good and evil framed by how power is used.
frames.concerns: Witchcraft vocabulary; same-sex couple (ACNA traditional, Episcopal affirming).

frames.aligns: Problems solved without violence (Common Sense Media); humility, community, care for the disabled.
frames.concerns: Conservative groups avoid fantasy media and witchcraft themes; worldly fashion and festival life; same-sex couple. MC USA families are much more open.

frames.aligns: Learning, agency, family love, service; consequences for choices.
frames.concerns: Occult and spirit themes are avoided in the tradition, though fantasy is commonly enjoyed; same-sex couple (The Family: A Proclamation).

frames.aligns: Inclusion, disability access, critique of gatekeeping, a same-sex couple shown with dignity, assault victims believed (ch. 49).
frames.concerns: Body horror; memory erasure of children.

frames.aligns: Care for health, family love, responsibility.
frames.concerns: Magic in stories is a common concern in the tradition; witches as heroes; same-sex couple. No spirits of the dead shown (to verify).
Magic and witchcraft in entertainment are widely avoided (jw.org counsel, Galatians 5:19-21); same-sex couple.

frames.aligns: Thought and creativity shape outcomes; love and inclusion outlast fear.
frames.concerns: Mind control (memory erasure) resembles what the tradition calls "animal magnetism," though the story treats it as troubling; body horror invites fear.

frames.aligns: Responsibility (teshuvah after harm), honoring a parent, care for the disabled, the gravity of sexual abuse (ch. 49).
frames.concerns: Sorcery forbidden (Deuteronomy 18:10-11): Haredi families often avoid fantasy magic, Modern Orthodox families are more accepting; same-sex couple.

frames.aligns: Learning valued for all; tikkun olam; dignity of the disabled; victims believed.
frames.concerns: Fantasy sorcery generally accepted; little to raise.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy, justice, inclusion, critique of secret power.
Responsibility, knowledge sought for good, care for parents, condemnation of sexual abuse; no polytheism shown.
frames.concerns: Sihr is forbidden, and magic shown positively is a concern (frame guide); same-sex couple. Modesty concerns are low.

frames.aligns: Duty to one's teacher (guru-shishya), karma of actions (Coco's mistake), ahimsa in nonviolent solutions.
Right intention, non-harm, compassion, the suffering caused by craving and secrets (Qifrey's revenge).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; body horror as "tamasic" content for some families.

frames.aligns: Seva (service), equality of women and men, defense of the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: The Gurus rejected magic and superstition, so heroic spellcasting may be discussed; little else.

frames.aligns: Education for all, unity, equality of women and men, non-violence, the arts as service.
frames.concerns: Same-sex couple (Bahá'í teaching limits sexual relations to marriage of a man and a woman); occult discouraged.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), gratitude (Tetia's love of thanking people), purity of intention, craft as near-sacred.
Witches portrayed as good, careful and creative; "harm none" echoes in the ban on harmful magic; The Wild Hunt reads the gatekeeping as a picture of suppressed folk healing.
frames.concerns: The magic is a secular craft rather than a religion; witches also run an exclusionary, memory-wiping institution.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be competent, do not harm.
frames.concerns: Memory and mind manipulation are central, framed as troubling.

frames.aligns: Inclusion, disability access, a canon gay couple, assault survivors believed, critique of gatekept power (Common Sense Media; Anime Feminist).
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist (2020) flags an "able-bodied savior" pattern in the Tartah arc.

frames.aligns: Magic as learnable craft, open to anyone (Wrong Every Time: "Magic is available to everyone"); reason, responsibility and prudence with powerful tools.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; magic is plainly fiction.

frames.aligns: Respect for teachers, apprenticeship and craft; personal responsibility; prudence about dangerous power; families honored.
