frames.concerns: Some concern about witchcraft themes; a same-sex couple; the story's sympathy for questioning institutions.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth, justice, free search for truth, inclusion.
Free inquiry and suspicion of authority that hoards knowledge; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2).
frames.concerns: The rebels who break the rules are mostly villains who harm children's bodies (Euini, ch. 18-23).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Disputes go to rules and courts (the Knights Moralis arrest the assaulter, ch. 49). Agott's need to defend her family name is shown as a burden she grows out of (vol. 2).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Balanced: the story shows why magic needs limits (ch. 1, ch. 63) but also the cruelty of total control (memory erasure, children wiped).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Coco's mother matters, but the core bonds are chosen ones (atelier, friends, Dagda as foster father), and help goes to strangers (Custas, the town of Ezrest).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teacher-apprentice respect is real, but elite gatekeeping and the "unknowing" class line are questioned (The Wild Hunt; Anime Feminist).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Magic is a reasoned craft of design and testing; no religion is shown. The Pact's tradition is honored for its reasons, not as sacred in itself.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Creativity, tolerance, accommodation and following one's dream (Coco) are central.

folkways.japan: The master-apprentice system (deshi), respect for craft and quiet group cooperation reflect Japanese norms; the European-styled setting and diverse cast are the creator's deliberate choice (Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: Beneath the Tangles: "Coco's coming of age never involves anything black and white." No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about access, responsibility and power come through plot dilemmas, with both the law and its rebels given reasons and faults.

personified.ideology: Protective care mixed with secret revenge; ends justify means
Magic should belong to everyone, at any cost
A duty to save people that overrides law
Order and enforcement of the Pact

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (prudence), Pragmatism, Critical theory (access and gatekeeping), Communitarianism, Progressivism, Pagan/occult (as fantasy witchcraft).

entry.heading: Land of the Lustrous
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Pride and the will to control others lead to ruin (Phos's arc); love that does not abandon (Kongo); despair is shown as suffering, not freedom. Depicts evil without making it attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Salvation as annihilation of the soul, performed by a human-made god; respect for other religions (Nostra Aetate) differs from presenting their goal as the truth of the world. Suicide attempt and begging for death (CCC 2280-2283).

frames.aligns: Watchfulness over the passions: Phos's craving to matter grows into tyranny. Kongo's patient love.
frames.concerns: A machine-monk and a forcibly made god in a story about salvation; theosis is union with God, not extinction. Buddha-like sacred imagery shown with reverence for a non-Christian end.

frames.aligns: No sexual content to speak of; clear costs to lying and manipulation; loyalty among friends.
frames.concerns: Salvation in the story is non-Christian and ends all life (John 14:6). Genderless cast praised by progressive critics may concern some congregations. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: A Christian blogger finds Ezekiel 36:26 and Jeremiah 18:6 in the soul, flesh and bone split (Beneath the Tangles). Pride, lies and their consequences.
frames.concerns: Buddhist end goal presented as the world's real answer; no God beyond human-made ones.

frames.aligns: Spiritual reality is taken seriously, not mocked; despair answered by persistence.
frames.concerns: Prayer to a made god and Buddhist rites as the means of release; some families see such spiritual content as an "open door."

frames.aligns: Common grace: a serious work of art by a non-Christian about sin-like craving and its fruits.
frames.concerns: Salvation by a human-made mediator and by extinction; Buddha-like images. Largely free of the "lascivious" content the Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 lists.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; the theme of a self that cannot save itself by works or upgrades.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian salvation; despair and the suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: Empathy for all beings; growth through suffering; the consequences of pride.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule about books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; despair themes. Holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Imagination as a gift; good and evil framed by consequences; a literary, ambiguous work in the Lewis and Sayers tradition.
frames.concerns: Ending with no hope beyond nothingness.

frames.aligns: Phos's turn to violence and manipulation is shown destroying community. Kongo will not strike back at the Lunarians directly (to verify).
frames.concerns: Ongoing combat; separation from the world makes most popular media a concern for Old Order groups.

frames.aligns: Little sexual content or language; loyalty and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Gender as eternal identity (The Family: A Proclamation to the World) differs from a sexless cast; salvation as extinction rather than exaltation. For the Strength of Youth asks what invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the marginal ("useless" Phos, the outcast Cinnabar); inclusive genderless cast; critique of manipulation by leaders.
frames.concerns: The despair and suicide scenes need care for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Little sexual content; consequences of pride.
frames.concerns: Souls of the dead active as Lunarians conflicts with the teaching that the dead sleep; "by beholding we become changed" applied to despair.

frames.aligns: Little sexual content; loyalty among friends.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian worship and prayer presented as true and effective; souls of the dead as active beings; a made god; ongoing violence (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Identity not reducible to material parts; the story's skepticism of the body as the self.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on breakage, fear and despair ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: No sexual content to speak of; serious moral consequences for lies and manipulation.
frames.concerns: A made god and its worship-like rites (avodah zarah); gender ambiguity; Haredi limits on secular media.
Non-Jewish salvation frame; the ending's bleakness.

frames.aligns: Empathy for all; tikkun olam echoes in Phos's wish to repair the world.
frames.concerns: The repair ends in erasing the world.

frames.aligns: Little sexual content (aside from short uniforms); pride shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: A god made by humans and prayed through (shirk); sacred-style imagery; gender ambiguity; scholars differ on images of living beings.

frames.aligns: Karma, rebirth, liberation and renunciation themes; dharma by role (hardness decides each gem's work).
frames.concerns: Liberation achieved by machine and force rather than knowledge and devotion; some may object to a "made god."

frames.aligns: The plot is Buddhist cosmology taken seriously: craving and attachment cause suffering (the Lunarians' desires; Phos's ambition); no-self (Phos's replaced parts); 108 desires; final renunciation (ch. 108). A Buddhist-themed reading calls it "a Buddhist as hell series" (Fumikoarmy blog). The creator's starting point was the Pure Land sutra (Current Obsession).
frames.concerns: Nirvana shown as erasure by mechanical prayer differs from many teachers' accounts of nirvana as neither annihilation nor existence. Buddha-like figures are a machine and a forcibly made god, which some may find careless. Violence and despair against the first precept's spirit.

frames.aligns: Ego (haumai) and attachment shown causing ruin; humility at the end; service to others.
frames.concerns: Liberation by machine prayer, not by Naam; despair themes.

frames.aligns: Unity, empathy across kinds of beings; no degrading sexual content.
Animist resonance: stones as living beings with feeling; purity and sincerity valued; Kongo's care for the gems.
frames.concerns: Buddhist rather than Shinto frame; shattering and death imagery (kegare).

frames.aligns: Living stones, cycles of destruction and new life (mineral life appears after the end, v13); empathy for non-human beings; no stereotyping of witches.
The self as more than the body (Phos keeps going through every replacement); memory central to identity.
frames.concerns: Despair and death-wish themes; little in The Way to Happiness is addressed directly.

frames.aligns: Gender-neutral cast praised by Anime Feminist and The Mary Sue; Sense of Gender Grand Prize; critique of manipulative leaders and of beings used as resources.
frames.concerns: Short-shorts uniforms (Anime Feminist); a single body type for the cast (The Mary Sue); suicide-attempt depiction for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Empathy beyond the human (the creator's stated aim); free inquiry into the self; no supernatural claims taught as fact outside the science-fiction frame.
frames.concerns: Religious salvation works literally within the story; the ending does not affirm human flourishing.

frames.aligns: A revered teacher; loyalty; the costs of rebellion and lies; no sexual content.
frames.concerns: Moral ambiguity and a bleak, nihilistic-seeming ending; genderless cast praised by progressive critics; authority shown keeping harmful secrets.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every being; free search for meaning; respectful use of a world religion.
Questioning a revered authority (Phos versus Kongo); self-determination over one's own body.
frames.concerns: Rebellion ends in disaster and self-erasure; individual will is not affirmed in the end.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No honor code or vendetta is celebrated. Phos's revenge on Cinnabar (ch. 89-94) is felt by fans as catharsis but leads to ruin. Worth is not tied to reputation; the "useless" gem matters.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The gems' ordered life under Kongo is shown warmly; Phos's freedom to remake everything costs dearly (ch. 80-97). Neither side is simply celebrated.

Civic vs kin.evidence: There is no kin: the gems are a chosen, school-like community. Loyalty is to friends and teacher, not blood.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hardness decides each gem's role and Kongo is sole authority; the story questions both but does not replace them.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Buddhist cosmology is sincere and literal within the story (Kongo's prayer, ch. 97), but performed by human-made technology and questioned by the creator ("There's a line somewhere").

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The search for one's own role and self is the engine of the plot; the ending turns toward letting the self go.

folkways.japan: The Buddhist vocabulary (nirvana, Enma, 49 days, 108 desires), the teacher-pupil bond and the Kodansha seinen setting reflect Japanese religious and cultural norms; readers outside Japan may see the Buddhist frame as the setting's furniture more than a message aimed at them, though here it carries the plot.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its strangeness and ambiguity (Manga Bookshelf: "its own thing"); fans argue over who was right, Kongo or Phos.
delivery.note: The religious and philosophical ideas are carried by plot structure and symbol rather than speeches, and the story leaves most verdicts to the reader.

personified.ideology: Release into nothingness by any means

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist), Existentialism, Transhumanism (body and identity), Nihilism (explored), Communitarianism.

series.title: The Fragrant Flower Blooms With Dignity
series.romaji: Kaoru Hana wa Rin to Saku

entry.heading: The Fragrant Flower Blooms With Dignity (Saka Mikami)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from seeing people as they are rather than as their label, from honest and patient kindness, and from working through fear and division together; love grows slowly and is tended.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person regardless of class (CCC 1700, 1935); charity across division; courtship that involves parents (vol. 8); reconciliation of enemies.
frames.concerns: Romance without a faith horizon; teen alone in a girl's room (vol. 19, to verify).

frames.aligns: Humility, meekness (Rintaro does not return blows), love shown in small service (baking), peacemaking.
frames.concerns: Romance as the center of life; guarding the senses applies lightly.

frames.aligns: "Man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7) is the premise; honesty, apology, honoring parents.
frames.concerns: Teen dating with little explicit boundary-setting; no faith frame. Each family decides.

frames.aligns: Breaking down "dividing walls of hostility" (Ephesians 2:14 echo) between groups; kindness to outsiders; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Hope and healing come from friends, not God; dating as a main source of meaning.

frames.aligns: Restoration of the low in spirit; warm community; no occult content.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on dating and appearance (piercings, dyed hair) vary by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a well-made, kind story; confession and apology; a lawful authority (school) persuaded rather than defied.
frames.concerns: Nothing lascivious reported (WLC Q139); teen romance focus.

frames.aligns: Vocation: baking, study, part-time work, parents' work honored (vol. 5). Confession and forgiveness among friends.
frames.concerns: Little; confessional families may weigh dating counsel.

frames.aligns: Social holiness on a small scale; inclusion of the despised; "do no harm" in Rintaro's restraint.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches more cautious about romance-centered media than UMC.

frames.aligns: Reconciliation, class barriers questioned, imagination used generously.
Nonresistance (Rintaro refuses to fight back), humility, peacemaking between communities, forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes a secular teen romance a concern for Old Order families; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Kindness, family-centered life, involving parents in courtship, honesty, ministering to the lonely.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth counsels care in dating as a teen; the private room scene (vol. 19) and piercings may be discussed.

frames.aligns: Justice across class lines, challenge to gender stereotypes, welcome of the outsider, care for bullying survivors.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; no LGBTQ representation reported.
Romance-centered entertainment (Ellen White on fiction exciting the passions); adornment counsel (piercings).

frames.aligns: Kindness, honesty, peaceableness, no spiritism or violence glorified.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsels dating only when old enough to marry; teen dating and being alone together (vol. 19).

frames.aligns: Love dissolves fear and prejudice; right thinking about others replaces false labels.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on self-doubt and sorrow; little else.

frames.aligns: Kavod habriyot (human dignity), avoiding lashon hara about the other school, honoring parents, hesed.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex teen dating and being alone together (yichud) are against halacha; many Haredi homes would not have it; Modern Orthodox families more selective.

frames.aligns: Dignity, lovingkindness, repairing relations between communities.
frames.concerns: Teen dating left to family values.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam on a small scale; dignity; challenging stereotypes.
Justice and dignity regardless of status (Qur'an 49:13: "the most noble... is the most righteous"); honoring parents; mercy; good character (akhlaq).
frames.concerns: The premise is unchaperoned dating; being alone together (khalwa, vol. 19); a likely kiss (vol. 14). No sexual content reported.

frames.aligns: Seva, respect for parents and teachers, humility, freedom from caste-like contempt for others.
frames.concerns: Romance in the student stage (brahmacharya) for some families.

frames.aligns: Right speech, compassion, non-violence, letting go of views about others.
Equality of all regardless of status (rejection of caste), seva, honest work (kirat karni), humility.
Elimination of prejudice is a core Bahá'í principle; unity; parents involved in the relationship.
frames.concerns: Teen dating with chastity left implicit.

frames.aligns: Makoto (sincerity), harmony restored, gratitude; New Year shrine visit shown naturally (vol. 14).
"Harm none," acceptance of difference, no stereotyping of pagans.
Communication resolves conflict; The Way to Happiness precepts (be worthy of trust, honor parents, respect others).
Anti-stereotype message, class awareness, gentle masculinity, consent-respecting slow romance, healthy parents (CSM).
frames.concerns: No LGBTQ representation reported; Kikyo's authorities are slow to change.

frames.aligns: Reason, dialogue and empathy settle conflict; meaning in human relationships.
frames.concerns: Characters' near-uniform goodness can feel idealized (MAL critics).

frames.aligns: Hard work, family business, respect for parents and teachers, gentlemanly conduct, courtship that faces the parents (vol. 8), change through proper channels (vol. 23).
frames.concerns: Teen dating normalized; the private room scene (vol. 19).

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person; justice and community; free search for understanding.
Challenges unjust institutional rules (Satanic Temple Tenet 2, justice); compassion (Tenet 1); reason over prejudice.
frames.concerns: Church of Satan readers may find the constant apologizing and self-effacement a weak model; little else.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inner, not reputational; Rintaro "doesn't fight back" when insulted (CSM); school "honor" is the problem the story dissolves.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Students meet against a school rule (vol. 22) but resolve it through teachers and the principal (vol. 23); rules are reformed, not discarded.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family matters (bakery, parents), but the story's hope is bridging two strangers' groups into one community.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Class rank between schools is critiqued; respect for parents and teachers remains.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life with customs kept lightly (shrine, Christmas, vol. 14); dialogue and reason settle conflict.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Tolerance, trust and being seen as oneself are the central values; study and work are present but not the point.

folkways.japan: The ranking of high schools by academic level, the stigma of "delinquent" boys' schools, single-sex private academies, part-time work and scholarships, the expectation of carrying on a family shop, New Year shrine visits and the constant apologizing and thanking critics note are Japanese norms that frame the story more than they form its message.

delivery.evidence: MAL critics: characters lose essence avoiding miscommunication, apologizing constantly; CSM: "An important theme is how stereotypes are harmful."
delivery.note: The anti-prejudice theme is stated often in dialogue, but the prejudiced side, including Kikyo's teacher Toki, is given understandable reasons.

personified.ideology: Do not judge by appearance; gentle masculinity
Distrust of the privileged other school

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Fullmetal Alchemist
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived within human limits. You accept loss, own your mistakes, work for what you get, give more than you take, and protect others instead of trying to become a god.

frames.aligns: Hubris punished; human life cannot be bought back or "measured"; body and soul as one unity (Sr. Orianne Dyck, Pauline.org, citing Theology of the Body); the seven deadly sins as villains (The Jesuit Post); evil never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Truth as a god figure unlike the Christian God; Edward's skepticism; souls trapped in objects; Cornello as a clerical fraud.

frames.aligns: Pride as the root passion: Father seeks to "eat God" (Beneath the Tangles) and is cast down; repentance of Scar and the soldiers; the body matters.
frames.concerns: Truth as a being that calls itself God; souls bound in matter; constant gore, a concern for guarding the senses (nepsis).

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; humility; hard work; a fake preacher exposed; family loyalty.
frames.concerns: Truth as a pantheistic god; the hero brushes aside God (UMC.org); souls in stones. Each congregation decides.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Edward's path as dependence, sonship and sacrificial love: "God is not our rival, He's our Father." Depicts sin without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian cosmology (Truth, "All is One"); grace comes through human love rather than God.

frames.aligns: Pride and false gods defeated; a fraudulent religion exposed.
frames.concerns: Alchemy, soul-binding, a "gate" to a god-being and souls of the dead harvested may read as occult "open doors"; the hero's skepticism. Views vary by church.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echo: the homunculi are Father's own sins cast off, yet he still embodies them (TV Tropes); common grace lets families value the craft; human limits upheld.
frames.concerns: Truth as a speaking image of "God" (second-commandment concern for some); fake clergy; salvation by sacrifice and effort.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel echo: equivalent exchange cannot save; Winry's answer to Edward points to giving all (Beneath the Tangles). Lawful authority restored after tyranny.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian cosmology; skepticism toward God. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: UMC.org writer: "The false gods that Ed fought against were of human origin and needed to be called out." Works of mercy, restoration of Ishval.
frames.concerns: The writer recalls a childhood "faith crisis" from Edward's dismissal of God. Holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Good and evil judged by framing, in the fantasy tradition of Lewis and Sayers; pride punished; just reform of a corrupt state.
frames.concerns: Truth as a non-Christian deity; violence.

frames.aligns: Sharp critique of state violence, war crimes and militarism; veterans' guilt; Edward refuses to kill.
frames.concerns: The heroes still fight, many as soldiers, and the military reforms rather than disbands. Conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: The body as essential to the soul; families bound beyond death; agency and accountability.
frames.concerns: Souls bound to armor and Stones; Truth as a god figure. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Genocide, racism and state cover-up condemned; the persecuted Ishvalans restored; structural sin made visible.
Pride punished; humility, hard work, family.
frames.concerns: Souls of the dead conscious inside Stones and armor conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; alchemy; gore.

frames.aligns: Love of family, honesty, exposing a false religion.
frames.concerns: Spiritism-like soul binding and a god figure at a "gate"; war and violence (Psalm 11:5); military heroes.

frames.aligns: The limits of material power; love outlasts loss.
frames.concerns: Death, bodily loss and fear shown as real and central; body horror.

frames.aligns: Human life is beyond price; the Ishvalan teaching that only God creates; golem-like limits on making life; genocide condemned and remembered.
frames.concerns: Truth as a being that claims to be God; attempts to raise the dead; violence; some modesty concerns (Lust). Many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Limits on human power; atonement by perpetrators; memory of atrocity.
Tikkun olam in the rebuilding of Ishval; critique of racism and state violence.
Ishvalan faith echoes Islamic teaching that only God creates; Father's attempt to become God condemned (shirk-like pride); a persecuted religious people honored; justice for the oppressed.
frames.concerns: Truth depicted as a speaking god figure; the attempt to raise the dead; Scar's killing in God's name; Ishvalans read by some as coded Middle Eastern (Wikipedia notes a Middle East parallel).

frames.aligns: "All is One, One is All" echoes non-dual thought; equivalent exchange has a karma-like feel; dharma of the protector.
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; some families apply the tamasic category to the gore.

frames.aligns: Craving for power and immortality destroys Father; Edward lets go of alchemy to save his brother; interdependence ("All is One"); compassion for enemies.
The five vices made into homunculi and defeated; honest labor; defense of the oppressed Ishvalans.
Harmony of science and religion; unity of peoples (Amestris, Ishval, Xing); work as worship; prejudice condemned.
Sincerity, gratitude, purity of motive; no disrespect to kami.
Respect for natural law and balance (equivalent exchange); alchemy shown as a craft, not demonized.
Way to Happiness precepts: do not murder, be industrious, honor parents.
Anti-racism, anti-militarism, genocide condemned, capitalism critique (Kotaku), capable women (The Mary Sue; Anime Feminist).
frames.concerns: Women outnumbered; the mother "fridged"; Lust's design; no LGBTQ characters (The Mary Sue).

frames.aligns: Reason and science used humbly; a fraudulent church exposed by evidence; human dignity and responsibility; the dead cannot return (The Dot and Line).
frames.concerns: Science shown as dangerous without ethics; a god-figure is real in the story.

frames.aligns: Hard work, family, responsibility, humility, courage, marriage; tyranny overthrown.
frames.concerns: The national military and its patriotism are the system under critique; religious skepticism.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of every person; justice for Ishval; free search for truth.
Skepticism, exposing religious fraud, defiance of an all-powerful ruler, science and compassion (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 5).
frames.concerns: The story punishes self-deification and praises humility, against Church of Satan self-as-god language.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge is questioned: Scar abandons his vendetta and Riza stops Mustang from killing Envy (v23, likely). Edward refuses to kill. Rights and dignity of Ishvalans matter more than personal honor.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story celebrates overthrowing an oppressive military order; but discipline, duty and lawful reform (not chaos) are honored.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Brotherhood and family drive the plot, but the climax is a civic fight for the whole nation and the restoration of Ishval (ch. 83-108).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Leaders who serve (Mustang, Olivier) are respected, while rule by a hidden elite is condemned; Ishvalans are restored as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Science, evidence and skepticism (Cornello exposed, ch. 1-2) lead, while sincere faith (Ishvala) is respected and a godlike Truth limits pride.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work and "those who don't work don't deserve to eat" (The Mary Sue) sit beside tolerance and learning across cultures (Xing, Ishval).

folkways.japan: Military rank, workplace duty and the Hokkaido farm ethic of hard work reflect Japanese norms; the European industrial setting and the Ainu-inspired Ishval story are Arakawa's own framing rather than a general Japanese value.

delivery.evidence: DVD Talk's Bobby Cooper first read the theme as anti-religious, then concluded Scar uses religion to justify murder (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The series states its themes in dialogue about equivalent exchange and God, and shows them through consequences for each side.

personified.ideology: Equivalent exchange turned to giving more than you take; skepticism of gods
Ishvalan faith turned to revenge, then rebuilding
Religion as a tool of control

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism (humble), Communitarianism, Transhumanism (critiqued), Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Pantheist / New Age.

entry.heading: Blue Period
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one you choose and work for: find what moves you, put in the hours, be honest about yourself, and let others be who they are.

values.presence: Recurring (central in the exam arc, ch. 1-25)

frames.aligns: Art as a path to beauty and truth (John Paul II, Letter to Artists, 1999); work and talents used well; mercy toward a suffering friend; a father's violence shown as wrong.
frames.concerns: Yuka's gender presentation and bisexuality are affirmed rather than examined (CCC 2357-2359; Dicastery documents, 2024, question gender ideology). Underage smoking and drinking early. A sacred image (Dead Christ) restaged as a student piece (ch. 27): judged by its framing.

frames.aligns: Ascetic-like discipline of practice; humility before the work; honesty with oneself.
frames.concerns: Gender seen as given in Orthodox teaching, so Yuka's arc reads against it; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes life-drawing nudity a concern for many families. Sacred images used as exercises (ch. 27).

frames.aligns: Hard work, honesty, kindness to a hurting friend; no occult content.
frames.concerns: A gender-nonconforming, bisexual character presented sympathetically (BF&M 2000, XVIII, usually a significant concern); underage smoking and drinking; nude figure study. Views vary by congregation under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing excess; vocation, diligence, compassion; the story is about calling and gifts, themes many churches "engage."
frames.concerns: Yuka's identity affirmed; casual teen vice early on; nudity in art study. Some churches affirming, most traditional.

frames.aligns: No demons, magic or occult: the "open door" concern is absent. Perseverance and passion.
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on sexuality and gender (AG position papers) against Yuka's affirmed arc; worldliness (smoking, drinking, hostess work); modesty standards and nude figure work.

frames.aligns: Common grace: good art by non-Christians may be valued (Kuyper). Vocation as service; honest depiction of sin's cost (the father's cruelty).
frames.concerns: Conservative churches (PCA, OPC) hold traditional teaching on gender; PC(USA) is affirming. WLC Q139 on "lascivious... pictures" raises the nudity question, though the nudity here is nonsexual.

frames.aligns: Vocation as a calling within daily work (Luther); entertainment as adiaphora; Christian freedom to value art.
frames.concerns: LCMS and WELS hold traditional views on gender; ELCA is affirming. Early teen vice.

frames.aligns: Growth through disciplined practice; compassion for the hurting; social holiness concerns about cruelty.
frames.concerns: UMC affirming since 2024; Global Methodist, Wesleyan and Nazarene traditional. Smoking and drinking; Wesley's rule on "diversions."

frames.aligns: A strong arts tradition; works judged by their moral vision; compassion and honesty.
frames.concerns: Episcopal Church affirming; ACNA traditional, so families will differ on Yuka's arc.

frames.aligns: Humility, nonviolence (almost no violence), care for a friend.
frames.concerns: Separation from the world: competitive prestige, self-expression as the goal, urban nightlife and nude study sit against plain living in conservative groups; MC USA families vary and some are moving toward affirming.

frames.aligns: Developing talents (parable of the talents); hard work; family love where present.
frames.concerns: Gender as eternal identity (The Family: A Proclamation, 1995) differs from Yuka's arc; Word of Wisdom concerns with teen smoking and drinking; modesty and nude figure study.

frames.aligns: Affirms Yuka's dignity; names a father's rejection as harm; values art as a way to explore human experience; compassion and justice.
frames.concerns: Early deadnaming and mocking of Yuka (Anime Feminist); worry that Yuka's suffering serves the hero's growth (ANN ep. 9).
Ellen White's caution about fiction and "exciting" entertainment; smoking and drinking against health teaching; traditional teaching on sexuality (General Conference statements); nude figure work.

frames.aligns: Honesty, hard work, kindness; no violence or spiritism to speak of.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality; homosexual acts and gender change are rejected in teaching, and Yuka's arc treats them sympathetically; teen smoking and drinking; ambition for worldly prestige.

frames.aligns: Thought and self-understanding shape life; love and courage over fear; healing of a friendship.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on anxiety, illness (hives) and despair; teen smoking and drinking. Less public teaching on gender (to verify).

frames.aligns: Diligence and learning; honoring a grandparent (Yuka's grandmother); condemnation of a parent's violence.
frames.concerns: Same-sex attraction and gender crossing (Leviticus 18:22; Deuteronomy 22:5 on cross-dressing) shown sympathetically; tzniut and nude figure study; many Haredi homes restrict secular media.

frames.aligns: Learning and craft; dignity of each person (CJLS 2006 on LGBTQ inclusion, views vary by congregation); critique of parental cruelty.
frames.concerns: Teen smoking and drinking; modesty values applied by families to nude study.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy; LGBTQ inclusion; tikkun olam echoes in care for a struggling friend.
frames.concerns: Early mocking and deadnaming; teen vice.

frames.aligns: Diligence, seeking excellence (ihsan), care for a grandmother, rejection of parental violence.
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on sexuality and gender against Yuka's affirmed arc; alcohol and smoking; images of living beings and nude figure drawing (lowering the gaze, Qur'an 24:30-31). Scholars differ on figurative art.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: following one's own nature and duty; art as a path (rasa theory); devotion to practice like a sadhana.
frames.concerns: Family duty (dharma) against Yatora's and Yuka's breaks with parental expectation; varying traditional views on gender.

frames.aligns: Mindful attention in seeing and drawing; impermanence and grief (Machiko); a temple setting treated respectfully (vols. 13-15).
frames.concerns: Craving for recognition and the exam ladder; intoxicants (fifth precept) early on. Views on gender vary and many traditions are accepting.

frames.aligns: Honest work (kirat karni); equality and dignity of each person; the five vices (ego, attachment) shown in exam rivalry and overcome.
frames.concerns: Tobacco is forbidden in the Rehat Maryada and alcohol rejected, both shown casually early; Akal Takht (2005) opposed same-sex marriage, though diaspora views vary.

frames.aligns: Arts as worship when done in service; rejection of prejudice; independent search for truth.
frames.concerns: Alcohol forbidden; teaching reserves sexual relations for a man-woman marriage; a "chaste and holy life" (Shoghi Effendi) and the hostess-bar setting.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), dedication to a craft, gratitude toward teachers and a grandparent; no disrespect to shrines or kami.
Self-knowledge, creativity, acceptance of diverse identities; "harm none" echoed in the critique of the father.
Hubbard praised the artist's role in society; competence and self-determinism; The Way to Happiness precepts on industriousness and competence.

A visible gender-nonconforming, bisexual character treated seriously (CBR; Queer Comics Database); family rejection named as harm (ANN: father "blatantly anti-trans/genderfluid"); critique of exam pressure and gatekeeping.
frames.concerns: Early deadnaming and mockery (Anime Feminist); young women "sometimes objectified" (Common Sense Media); worry that Yuka's suffering exists to move Yatora's story (ANN ep. 9); a MAL reviewer calls Yuka a "dated trope"; teen smoking and drinking.

frames.aligns: Meaning made through human effort, skill and friendship; free inquiry about art; empathy; no supernatural claims.
frames.concerns: Casual teen smoking and drinking; mental-health strain without much professional help shown.

frames.aligns: Discipline, merit, apprenticeship, respect for skilled teachers, the classical pursuit of beauty; no nihilism.
frames.concerns: Gender-nonconforming identity presented sympathetically to teen readers; underage vice; parental authority set aside for personal passion.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity (Yuka); free search for truth and meaning; critique of rejection and cruelty.
frames.concerns: Early mockery and deadnaming; the "device" concern (ANN).

frames.aligns: Nonconformity and self-determination; bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3); art that challenges authority; rejection of enforced "normal."

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent and not defended by force; Yatora apologizes for mocking Yuka (ch. 1-2; Anime Feminist), and Yakumo's collar-grab (vol. 15) is shown as a lapse, not a virtue.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Choosing one's own path against parents and norms is celebrated (Yatora, ch. 1-6; Yuka, v5), though within the discipline of practice and exams.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Friends, teachers and fellow artists carry the characters more than family; Yuka's family is the main source of harm, the grandmother the exception.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Good teachers are respected (Saeki); a cold professor (Inukai, vols. 12-13) and the exam ladder are questioned. Senpai-kohai ties are present but light.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Choice, reason and self-knowledge guide life; religion appears only as art history and setting (ch. 27; vols. 13-15).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression and tolerance are the goals, but security is taken seriously: hard work, fees, the mother's fear for Yatora's future.

folkways.japan: The entrance-exam system, prep-school (yobikō) culture, ronin students, senpai-kohai manners and parents' expectation of a stable career are Japanese norms the story uses as its setting; its own message pushes for personal choice within them.

delivery.evidence: ANN finds vol. 1 sometimes "how to"; reviewers praise Yuka's arc as serious. No opened review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series argues through Yatora's inner monologue and art lessons, letting the mother, rivals and professors make real counterpoints.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Pragmatism.

entry.heading: Kingdom
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A worthy life is lived for a great dream larger than oneself: courage, loyalty to comrades and a just king, and the will to rise from nothing, spent in a war the story frames as the price of a lasting peace.

content.framing: Mixed: battlefield killing is heroic; massacres and torture are condemned by the heroes

frames.aligns: Just-war questions are live: protecting noncombatants and sparing prisoners are upheld by the heroes (CCC 2313); loyalty, sacrifice, a ruler who seeks the common good.
frames.concerns: Conquest is the stated goal, which just-war teaching does not accept as a just cause (CCC 2309); war glory can be made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); constant bloodshed.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for others; mercy to the defeated; courage.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against 80 volumes of killing; the church's canons historically asked penance of soldiers who killed (St. Basil, Canon 13).

frames.aligns: Clear villains; courage, loyalty and keeping one's word; Romans 13 order under a ruler.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test against constant gore; pride and ambition ("greatest general under heaven") celebrated; no God in the moral world.

frames.aligns: Many evangelical readers can distinguish depicting war from endorsing atrocity; heroes protect the weak and spare prisoners.
frames.concerns: Glory-seeking as the hero's life goal; violence volume; peace made by human empire, not God.

frames.aligns: Little occult content; courage and perseverance.
frames.concerns: The Shiyuu clan's rites and a life-for-life ritual (likely v58-59; to verify) may weigh more for families wary of spiritual "open doors"; heavy violence.

frames.aligns: Total depravity shown plainly (Huan Yi, court intrigue); providence-like history; the magistrate's sword (WCF 23).
frames.concerns: The king's faith in human goodness ("light") runs against Reformed anthropology; glory without God; WLC Q139 concern on lascivious images (Queen Dowager scenes).

frames.aligns: Luther's "Whether Soldiers, Too, Can Be Saved" (1526) allows the soldier's vocation; order under law; Xin's duty as vocation.
frames.concerns: Wars of conquest fall outside Luther's defense of soldiers; violence level is a conscience matter.

frames.aligns: Concern for the poor and the ordinary soldier; merit over birth; Xin rises from servitude.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches may weigh the war-glory against Wesley's General Rules; the UMC Social Principles reject war as an instrument of policy.

frames.aligns: An epic in the line of historical novels; just-war tradition (Article 37 permits Christians to serve in wars).
frames.concerns: War of conquest glorified; little interior moral cost.

frames.aligns: Mercy to prisoners; criticism of cruelty; the cost of war is visible.
frames.concerns: Violence is the hero's path to honor and the story's means to peace; this is the core conflict with nonresistance (Schleitheim Art. 6).

frames.aligns: Moroni-like defense of the people; loyalty, courage, rising through righteous effort.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: entertainment that invites the Spirit; constant killing; conquest as goal (contrast D&C 98:16, "renounce war and proclaim peace").

frames.aligns: Merit over birth; women commanders; concern for prisoners and civilians.
frames.concerns: Empire-building and authoritarian unity presented as the hope of history; questions about rehabilitating a famous tyrant (MAL review).
"By beholding we become changed": prolonged battlefield killing; Adventist noncombatancy contrasts with the hero's calling.

frames.aligns: Corrupt human rulers and court intrigue exposed.
frames.concerns: Violent entertainment is discouraged (Psalm 11:5); the story celebrates a human government's war and political loyalty, which Witnesses avoid.

frames.aligns: Unity and order sought; fear faced with courage.
frames.concerns: Long dwelling on killing and death; "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Mercy to captives and noncombatants echoes rules of war (Deut. 20:10, 20:19); justice under law; honoring the dead.
frames.concerns: Glorified bloodshed; immodest Queen Dowager scenes (tzniut); time on secular media.

frames.aligns: Law as the basis of a just society; dignity of prisoners.
Tikkun olam in the dream of ending war; merit over birth.
frames.concerns: Peace by conquest; a tyrant's image softened; human cost borne by the conquered.

frames.aligns: Islamic rules of war forbid killing prisoners, women, children and noncombatants (hadith of Abu Bakr's instructions), matching Xin and Ying Zheng's stance; justice and loyalty.
frames.concerns: Wars of expansion for glory; the Queen Dowager's affair and some nudity (lowering the gaze, 24:30-31); drinking.

frames.aligns: Kshatriya dharma: the warrior's duty to fight for a righteous king (Gita 2:31-33); loyalty, courage, a dharmic ruler; adharmic cruelty (Huan Yi) condemned.
frames.concerns: Tamasic gore; the desire for personal glory over detached action (Gita 2:47).

frames.aligns: Compassion for prisoners; the suffering of war shown; impermanence of generals and kingdoms.
frames.concerns: The first precept (non-harm); peace through killing is not the Buddhist path.

frames.aligns: The saint-soldier (sant-sipahi) ideal of fighting to protect the weak; equality of rank by merit.
frames.concerns: Fighting for conquest and glory differs from fighting against oppression (Zafarnama: the sword is lawful only when all other means fail); ego and anger (Huan Yi) shown at length.

frames.aligns: The unity of a fragmented world and an end to war as the goal.
frames.concerns: Unity by conquest conflicts with Bahá'í teaching of unity through consultation and collective security; violence against a "chaste and holy life."

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), loyalty and honoring the dead; a Japanese retelling of Chinese history.
frames.concerns: Blood and death (kegare) throughout; no kami or shrines.

frames.aligns: Mountain tribes and the Shiyuu clan shown with respect; strong women; honor among warriors.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" contrasts with the war ethic.

frames.aligns: Leadership, purpose and survival; The Way to Happiness ("Do not murder"; "Support a government designed and run for all the people").
frames.concerns: Killing as heroic; little treatment of trauma.

frames.aligns: Women generals and strategists; meritocracy against hereditary privilege; prisoners' rights.
frames.concerns: Rehabilitates an autocrat and frames conquest as progress; critics see war glorified and the image of the First Emperor "laundered" (MAL review); gender flips of historical men may read as tokenism or as welcome.

frames.aligns: Human reason, law and merit build order; the king's faith in human "light"; no supernatural rescue.
frames.concerns: Cruelty on a large scale; ends-justify-means reasoning for 15 years of war.

frames.aligns: Duty, loyalty, courage, hierarchy earned by merit, law and order, honoring the fallen; respect for worthy enemies.
frames.concerns: Violence level; a revolutionary centralizing state that ends old aristocracies is not a traditional ideal; little family or faith.

frames.aligns: Dignity of prisoners; a dream of world peace.
frames.concerns: Peace imposed by conquest; authoritarian unity.

frames.aligns: Self-made rise from slavery; challenge to aristocratic authority; strength and ambition (Satanic Bible); harm to children condemned by the heroes.
frames.concerns: Absolute monarchy and loyalty to a king; the Satanic Temple's Tenets on compassion and bodily autonomy vs. massacres.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Warriors' honor, vows to the dead and avenging fallen comrades drive the plot (Xin carries Piao's and Wang Qi's wills); but the king's law over private revenge is upheld (Huan Yi warned, ch. 671-701).

Order vs freedom.evidence: A strong state, uniform law and military discipline are celebrated; Li Si on law as the expression of the people's hopes (Business Insider Japan; Bureaucrats arc, ch. 486-495, v45, likely).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Law applies to all and merit replaces birth, yet loyalty to one's unit and lord is personal and fierce (Fei Xin unit).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank, king and generals deserve deference, but anyone can climb by merit (servant to general, ch. 642).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion is nearly absent; strategy, law and reason guide the state; old aristocracies are swept aside.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security, hard training and sacrifice come first; Xin's dream is personal but lived through duty.

folkways.japan: The senpai-kohai-like bonds inside the army, the group loyalty of the Fei Xin unit and the honoring of the dead through inherited will reflect Japanese norms; the portrait of the First Emperor as an enlightened ruler is a Japanese reading of Chinese history, different from the traditional Confucian verdict of tyranny (Sixth Tone).

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers note chapters are often "mostly speeches"; one says the series "launders" the First Emperor's image; Lü Buwei and Li Mu get serious hearings.
delivery.note: Ying Zheng states the unification ideal in set-piece speeches and debates, while rivals like Lü Buwei and Li Mu are argued with rather than mocked.

personified.ideology: Unification by conquest and rule by law to end war
Coexistence of the states; defense of Zhao
Rage against the powerful; atrocity as method

entry.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism (affirmed in a benevolent form), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Might makes right (explored and partly affirmed), Utilitarianism, Confucian ethics (explored). Legalism, the Qin state philosophy Ying Zheng and Li Si stand for, is not on the list; it is carried by the Collectivism/authoritarianism and Pragmatism rows (my own framing).

series.title: Don't Toy With Me, Miss Nagatoro
series.native: イジらないで、長瀞さん

entry.heading: Don't Toy With Me, Miss Nagatoro
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found by letting someone close enough to see your weak points, and growing braver through it. Confidence, honesty and showing your feelings are rewarded; hiding behind shyness or teasing is outgrown.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance and teasing); Neutral (fan service gags); Shown with consequences (the vol. 20 nude-drawing lie)
Endorsed early; softened; partly shown with consequences

frames.aligns: Growth from shame to courage; apology and reconciliation after a lie (vol. 20); love that seeks the other's good in later volumes.
frames.concerns: Inter Mirifica 7: wrong should not be made attractive; here sexual teasing of a minor and humiliation are played as charming. Chastity and modesty (CCC 2521-2524); cohabitation as the ending.

frames.aligns: Humility; repentance and forgiveness in vol. 20.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis): the art invites looking at teen bodies; nude modeling (vol. 15). Mockery as a passion, not a virtue.

frames.aligns: Courage, honesty and apology in the later volumes.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on many pages; a Christian blogger calls the anime "on the border between 'soft porn' and straight up pornography" (Holy Anime Wars). Cohabitation ending. Families decide under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: A shy outsider gains confidence; truth-telling and repentance restore the relationship (vol. 20).
frames.concerns: Depicting versus endorsing: early bullying and sexual teasing are endorsed by framing; sexual content involving minors; cohabitation.

frames.aligns: Restoration of a wounded boy's confidence.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty and separation from worldliness; media as an "open door" to lust.

frames.aligns: Common grace in Senpai's craft and study; confession of wrong in vol. 20.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 names "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the nude modeling and fan service are the test case.

frames.aligns: Confession and forgiveness (vol. 20); vocation in art and study.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment: "lead a sexually pure and decent life"; cohabitation plan. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth in courage and honesty; friends who help.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule to avoid books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; humiliation as humor. Holiness churches would avoid it; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: the cruelty fades and honest love wins; repentance after a lie.
frames.concerns: Fan service of minors; early bullying played for laughs; cohabitation. Episcopal and ACNA families weigh these differently.

frames.aligns: Humility, a quiet young man, reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; immodesty throughout; humiliation as humor. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Developing talents (art, judo); honesty and apology.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: media that does not invite the Spirit; the law of chastity in thought; cohabitation before marriage.

frames.aligns: A shy outsider valued; honesty and repair after harm.
frames.concerns: Bullying normalized as affection; consent and the sexualization of minors (CSM).

frames.aligns: Diligence in study and training; honesty.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment "of the highest quality"; "by beholding we become changed" weighs on the fan service; cohabitation.
jw.org counsel to avoid entertainment featuring immorality and "uncleanness" (Galatians 5:19-21); sexual teasing and nudity played for laughs; cohabitation.

frames.aligns: Fear and shame overcome by love; Senpai's thought changes from defeat to confidence.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on sensual images and on humiliation as mental influences to guard against.

frames.aligns: Teshuva-like repair after a lie (vol. 20); perseverance.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: teen sexual teasing and nudity throughout; ona'at devarim (wounding words) and embarrassing another in public treated as humor; cohabitation.

frames.aligns: Repair of a wrong; growth of courage.
frames.concerns: Shaming others as humor; modesty; sexualization of minors.

frames.aligns: Emotional honesty; relationship repaired through apology; growth of a shy boy.
frames.concerns: Bullying as affection; sexualization of minors; informed autonomy leaves it to families.

frames.aligns: Apology and honesty; perseverance in study and sport.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and modesty: the series is built on display; unchaperoned teen intimacy; mockery (Qur'an 49:11, "let not a people ridicule another people"); cohabitation.

frames.aligns: Effort in study and sport; loyalty of friends.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's rajasic and tamasic categories to sensual and mocking media; brahmacharya for students.

frames.aligns: Right speech learned the hard way; a relationship healed by honesty; compassion grows from mockery.
frames.concerns: Harsh speech as humor; sensual imagery as feed for the mind.

frames.aligns: Honest effort (kirat karni); humility in Senpai.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) and ahankar (ego) played for laughs.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness and reconciliation; service among friends.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" and against degrading entertainment; backbiting-style mockery.

frames.aligns: Shrine visits shown with ordinary respect (ch. 72; Kyoto trip); sincerity (makoto) in the final confession.
frames.concerns: Little doctrinal concern; harmony is broken by mockery in early arcs.

frames.aligns: Self-expression and body confidence; mutual care in later volumes.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" runs against humiliation and unwanted touching.

frames.aligns: Competence through practice; communication solves problems (vol. 20).
frames.concerns: The Way to Happiness precepts on decency and good example; sexualized teen art.

frames.aligns: A role-reversal romance with an assertive girl athlete; a shy boy's growth; honesty repairs harm.
frames.concerns: Consent: unwanted sexual touching and humiliation framed as flirting (CSM); bullying normalized; sexualization of minors; CSM finds "no positive parental or teacher roles."

frames.aligns: Meaning from art, effort, friendship and love; no supernatural framing; honest repair.
frames.concerns: Critical thinking about bullying-as-affection and sexualized teen art.

frames.aligns: Hard work, a young man learning courage and responsibility, honesty.
frames.concerns: The good, the true and the beautiful versus sexualized display of teens; cohabitation rather than marriage; a dominant girl and a weak boy as comedy.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the mocked boy; growth in respect and honesty.
frames.concerns: Consent and age-appropriateness; how girls' and boys' bodies are portrayed.

frames.aligns: Indulgence and self-expression without shame; a weak boy becoming self-assertive; personal responsibility after a lie.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules counsel not making sexual advances without the "mating signal"; Nagatoro's early advances and touching; concern about the sexualization of minors.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Embarrassment and "losing face" drive the comedy, and Senpai learns to stand up for himself, but the resolution is through honest talk and apology (vol. 20), not saving face.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Clubs are defended against the student council and the president's closure plan (Wikipedia); rules are mostly obstacles.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Peer friendships and the art club matter more than family; Nagatoro's sister and brother appear briefly (ch. 59).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai-kohai rank is inverted for laughs, then replaced by a partnership of equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular outlook; shrine visits are customs (ch. 72), and Senpai chooses self-work over prayer.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Art, self-confidence, showing one's feelings and personal goals (arts university, judo) are celebrated.

folkways.japan: Senpai-kohai seniority, club culture, student councils, entrance-exam pressure, New Year shrine visits and the "teasing girl" romantic-comedy type are Japanese school norms and genre habits more than a message aimed at readers.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Farris says the bullying premise becomes "practically an afterthought"; no review found calls the series preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about courage and honesty grows out of the romance itself, while the early teasing is presented with little critique inside the story.

personified.ideology: Quiet growth into courage and honesty
Teasing as a way of showing love

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism (self-making through risk), Hedonism (play and pleasure), Classical virtue ethics (courage and honesty, late).

entry.heading: Slam Dunk
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Anyone can change: a hot-tempered delinquent and a bitter dropout find themselves through hard practice, humble basics and a team that takes them back. Talent matters only when it serves the team, and you are not finished until you give up.

content.framing: Played for comedy early; shown with consequences in the Mitsui arc

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; rare inside

frames.aligns: Conversion and mercy: Mitsui's tearful return and Anzai's forgiveness (v8) echo the prodigal son (Luke 15). Gifts serve the common good of the team. Violence is not made attractive in the gym arc, where it costs Mitsui years (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Early fights and headbutts are comic; frequent swearing; "Gorilla" name-calling and human dignity (CCC 2479 on detraction, from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Repentance (metanoia) as a turning of life: Mitsui and Sakuragi. Ascetic labor (podvig): 20,000 shots. Humility before an elder.
frames.concerns: Nepsis asks what comic brawling and constant insults form in a reader.

frames.aligns: Repentance and a new life (2 Corinthians 5:17) in Mitsui; perseverance (Hebrews 12:1); confession of fault (Sakuragi's shaved head, ch. 133).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test on profanity and on fighting played for laughs. Soul liberty: families decide.

frames.aligns: A clear redemption arc that many evangelicals would "engage": the broken athlete welcomed back. Encouragement within the team. Plugged In recommends the film for its perseverance and family reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Language (Plugged In counts in the film); a "rough bullying scene"; early violence.

frames.aligns: Boldness, passion, never giving up; no occult practice.
frames.concerns: Nicknames "devil" and "Buddha"; the film's cartoon devil and shrine prayer (Plugged In) are minor, but families who see media as an "open door" may note them.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a well-made story about sin's cost and restoration; vocation in each position; the fruit of disciplined labor.
frames.concerns: Sport as idol; Larger Catechism concerns are minimal here (no lascivious content).

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; law and gospel visible in Mitsui's arc (he sees his wrong, then is forgiven).
frames.concerns: LCMS and WELS families may weigh language more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Transformation of character over time; accountability in community; holiness as love of teammates.
frames.concerns: Wesley's test of diversions; holiness churches may weigh swearing and brawls.

frames.aligns: Clear moral framing: the gang brawl is the low point, and the story moves away from it.
Humility, yielding to the team, and the end of fighting as part of Mitsui's change (he vows never to fight again; Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: The guide's central concern, violence shown as heroic, applies to Sakuragi's punches in the gym fight (TV Tropes) and the comic headbutts. Old Order groups avoid such media; competition sits uneasily with nonresistance.

frames.aligns: Repentance, hard work, goal-setting, respect for leaders; no substance use by players. For the Strength of Youth asks for entertainment that invites the Spirit, and the redemption arc fits.
frames.concerns: Profanity and fighting; Yazawa's drug-related death (backstory).

frames.aligns: Second chances for an outsider; a team that includes a "punk" and a dropout; mentor who protects the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Women mainly as fan and managers; the colorist "Gorilla" nickname (Common Sense Media).

frames.aligns: Discipline, perseverance and redemption; no substance use by players.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": comic brawling and competitive passion are the series' fuel; Ellen White warned against amusements that excite the passions (from general knowledge; to verify). Playing through injury vs. health stewardship.

frames.aligns: Reformed conduct (Mitsui gives up violence), cooperation, respect for elders; no occult practice.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsels avoiding entertainment that features violence God hates (Psalm 11:5); the gang fight and comic headbutts are central early. Counsel against a competitive spirit (Galatians 5:26; from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Overcoming fear and limitation through right thinking: "if you give up, the game is over" (Anzai's line, fan wiki).
frames.concerns: Injury, pain and a heart attack are central plot points; the medical and rehab framing (Sakuragi's months of rehab, TV Tropes) differs from the church's prayer-based healing; members decide for themselves.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah (return) in Mitsui; respect for a teacher; effort (hishtadlut). Pirkei Avot 4:1 on the strong person as one who conquers his impulse fits Sakuragi's growth and Santos's reading that a boy must "conquer himself."
frames.concerns: Many Haredi homes restrict secular media; nivul peh (crude speech) and insults in English versions; comic violence.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah, mentorship, community; kind speech is the weak point.
Dignity of the outsider; repair (tikkun) of a broken team.
Tawba (repentance) in Mitsui; sabr (patience) in loss; ihsan in practice; brotherhood.
frames.concerns: Profanity; fighting played for laughs; romantic chasing and locker-room partial nudity in the anime (lowering the gaze, 24:30-31). Scholars differ on images and entertainment.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: each player finds his role (Sakuragi as rebounder); disciplined action (karma yoga); the teacher (guru) who transforms students.
frames.concerns: Rajasic anger and pride are strong early.

frames.aligns: Anzai as the "White-Haired Buddha": calm, compassion and patience after suffering; impermanence of each tournament; right effort.
frames.concerns: The story runs on craving to win and on anger in early volumes; ego is softened but not let go. Lay observance days exclude entertainment.

frames.aligns: Haumai (ego) overcome: Rukawa learns to pass, Sakuragi learns basics; chardi kala after defeat; seva to the team.
Unity and cooperation; transformation of character; excellence as service.
frames.concerns: Fighting and coarse language against the "chaste and holy life" (to verify wording).

frames.aligns: Makoto (sincerity) of effort; gratitude to the mentor; harmony (wa); the film's shrine prayer is treated respectfully (Plugged In).
Self-knowledge and personal growth; community. "Harm none" is broken by the brawls, which the story moves past.
"Be competent" (The Way to Happiness); group dynamic; no psychiatric content.
Second chances for a delinquent; emotional openness among boys (crying, apology); the film's grief story and respected female manager (Common Sense Media).
frames.concerns: Women largely in support roles; the colorist "Gorilla" nickname; comic violence and playing through injury (AAP guidance on youth sports injury, from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Human effort, practice and reason transform people; no supernatural help; failure as learning (film: "losing will be an asset," Common Sense Media).
Discipline, respect for a wise elder, duty to team and school, hard work over shortcuts, personal responsibility, redemption through effort.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; mild language and comic fighting.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the "punk" and the dropout; interdependent web of a team.
Self-development and earned respect; Sakuragi's self-confident "genius" persona; no false piety. TST tenets on correcting mistakes fit Mitsui's arc.
frames.concerns: The story subordinates the self to the team and honors humility; the Church of Satan's individualism sits uneasily. (Range: TST closer to A; Church of Satan closer to C.)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Early chapters celebrate answering insult with fists and headbutts (v1-2; TV Tropes); the gym fight (v7-8) answers honor with violence. But the story moves disputes onto the court, and Mitsui's change includes a vow not to fight (Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Discipline and basics under Anzai and Akagi; delinquent freedom is shown as a dead end (Mitsui, v8).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty goes to team and school, and to Sakuragi's band of friends (Mito's "Sakuragi Legion"); families mostly offstage in the manga.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai-kohai, captain and coach are deferred to; but Sakuragi, a beginner, earns a starting role, and Anzai leads gently.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith shapes choices; practice and strategy win. School club traditions keep it from the far end.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work and endurance are central; so are Sakuragi's flamboyant self-expression and love of the game.

folkways.japan: The furyō delinquent style, senpai-kohai deference, school club teams, head-shaving as an apology (ch. 133) and the third-years' last tournament are Japanese school norms shown as setting. The "Gorilla" nickname reflects 1990s Japanese colorism, as Common Sense Media notes. The story's own message (second chances, team over self) is less hierarchical than the Confucian cluster's placement; Confucian ties with Orthodox Europe by distance.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Kimlinger calls it "a fun read" without depth early; Common Sense Media stresses teamwork and humility.
delivery.note: Lessons arrive through games and character turns, and rival teams' approaches are treated with respect.

personified.ideology: Bitterness and gang life, then repentance
Patient faith in players; never give up

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism; Might makes right and Nihilism critiqued.

entry.heading: The Climber (Kokou no Hito)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A life is worth living when you give all your strength to something, but no one can live entirely alone. The rope that ties climbers together, and in the end a family, is what brings a person back down the mountain.

frames.aligns: The ending favors marriage, a child and life over a deadly goal; isolation is shown as a wound; lust is resisted.
frames.concerns: Reckless risk to life (CCC 2288-2290 on care for health and life); Takemura's rope cut and the suicide-attempt backstory (CCC 2280-2283); Yumi's arc.

frames.aligns: Ascetic endurance, struggle with the passions ("Worldly desires", ch. 42), solitude that ends in communion with others.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses makes the sexual scenes and dark imagery a concern; despair shown at length.

frames.aligns: Perseverance; resisting temptation; family at the end.
frames.concerns: Sexual content (Philippians 4:8); despair without reference to God. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin and despair without endorsing them; redemption through love and belonging.
frames.concerns: No source of hope beyond human ties; sexual content.

frames.aligns: Clear cost of obsession; family restored.
frames.concerns: Hallucinations and dark visions; sexual temptation scenes. Little occult content.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value the craft; human pride ("Sinful pride", ch. 101) is shown failing.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures for the Yumi chapters; WLC Q136 on risking life needlessly.

frames.aligns: Vocation in marriage and work at the end; human limits exposed.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; despair. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Discipline, perseverance, growth toward love of others.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: obsession and isolation are shown as costly; love and belonging win.
Humility before creation; community and family at the end.
frames.concerns: Individual glory and competition are the engine of the story; worldly media in general. Conservative groups avoid it; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as the place of belonging; marriage and a child redeem a lonely life.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; risk to life. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Mental-health honesty; loneliness taken seriously; critique of media sensationalism.
frames.concerns: Treatment of women (ANN; MAL); untreated depression.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, temperance at the end, family.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": the despair, sexual scenes and death imagery. Health message runs against reckless risk.
Sexual content (Galatians 5:19-21); reckless risk to life, which members are taught to respect as sacred. Little spiritism.
Long dwelling on fear, despair, illness and death.

frames.aligns: Choosing life and family at the end (Deuteronomy 30:19).
frames.concerns: Needless danger is forbidden (Deuteronomy 4:15, ushmartem); suicide-adjacent scenes; tzniut makes the sexual chapters a concern. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr) and endurance; family at the end.
frames.concerns: Throwing oneself into destruction (Qur'an 2:195) and the prohibition of suicide (4:29) for the risk and the rope cut; lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the sexual chapters.

frames.aligns: Tapas (discipline) and detachment; a householder stage that follows a seeker's stage.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the despair and lust.

frames.aligns: Craving and attachment (to summits, to recognition) cause suffering; chapter titles use karma, rebirth, worldly desires, liberation.
frames.concerns: Lust scenes; risk to life. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: Honest work, endurance; ego (haumai) and lust shown as struggles.
frames.concerns: Lust scenes; ego as the hero's fuel for much of the story.

frames.aligns: Service and unity, solitude overcome by love; work as worship.
frames.concerns: Sexual content against a "chaste and holy life".

frames.aligns: Reverence and fear before mountains; sincerity (makoto); purity motifs; ancestors and family.
frames.concerns: Death on mountains as impurity; little to raise in message.

frames.aligns: Respect for nature's power; harm none, including oneself.
Survival across the dynamics, from self to family; taking care of oneself (Way to Happiness).
frames.concerns: Self-destructive risk; depression shown without the Church's frame.

frames.aligns: Honest look at depression and isolation; critique of sensational media.
frames.concerns: Women characters (ANN's Dee; MAL); unclear stance on toxic masculinity; untreated mental illness; suicide-adjacent scenes need safe-messaging context.

frames.aligns: Meaning made in a finite life by effort and human bonds; nature's indifference faced honestly.
Discipline, endurance, self-reliance, marriage and fatherhood as the answer to drift.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; long despair; gratuitous risk.

frames.aligns: Free search for meaning; interdependence (the rope); worth of every person.
Individualism, self-mastery and rejection of social conformity in most of the story (Church of Satan).
frames.concerns: Ends by choosing belonging over the solitary self; self-destructive risk runs against self-preservation.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Mori climbs for himself, not to answer insults; rivals' pride and Niimi's fight to clear his father's name (ch. 55, 81) are shown as costly.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Solo climbing against warnings and club rules (ch. 10-14, 21-24); freedom from others is the hero's goal for most of the story.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Little civic life; the ending places worth in a wife and child (ch. 129 "Mountains or family"; final chapter).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Mentors (Onishi, Adachi) are respected for care, not rank; the K2 team's leaders are not revered.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith practice; Buddhist words as metaphor; reverence for mountains.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Climbing as self-expression and meaning, balanced by bare survival, poverty and frostbite.

folkways.japan: Pressure to fit in at school and work, the outsider who cannot read the group, a teacher as moral guide, and taking the wife's family surname in marriage (mukoyōshi-style naming) are Japanese social norms in the setting rather than the story's message.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Dee: unclear whether it critiques or endorses toxic masculinity. Reviewers praise visual metaphor; none call it preachy.
delivery.note: The message comes through visual metaphor, interior monologue and consequences rather than speeches.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism (critiqued), Stoicism, Classical virtue ethics.

entry.heading: The Flowers of Evil
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Sin is shown as enslaving, not freeing; guilt, confession (the note in ch. 8) and a long reckoning lead toward reconciliation. Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7). Baudelaire, a poet steeped in Catholic ideas of sin, is the frame (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Nakamura's nihilism is voiced with sympathy and never answered in faith; the planned suicide (CCC 2280-2283); sexual content involving minors, including an assault (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: A clear picture of the passions (lust, pride, despair) growing from one act. Repentance-like turning in the second half.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer; the passions are explored at length with no ascetic remedy. Nepsis (guarding the senses) makes the voyeurism, assault and suicide plan a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences are shown honestly; confession and a changed life later.
frames.concerns: No gospel hope; nihilism voiced sympathetically; vulgar language. Under Philippians 4:8 the sexual content and suicide plan are a heavy concern. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: A realistic fallen world in which hidden sin grows and is exposed; restoration through honesty. Many in this tradition distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer; Nakamura's contempt for everyone as "shitbugs" is never refuted. Explicitness involving minors is high even for families who engage culture.

frames.aligns: No occult or demonic content; a vivid picture of bondage to shame.
frames.concerns: No spiritual deliverance offered; a dark, oppressive atmosphere. Holiness standards make the sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has a strong echo: Nakamura's claim that everyone hides perversion; the "respectable" Saeki is no exception. Common grace lets adults value serious art.
frames.concerns: No grace named. WLC Q139 makes the sexual imagery a heavy concern; the suicide plan as self-murder (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Law at work: guilt crushes Kasuga until he confesses and is accepted (Saeki, later Tokiwa).
frames.concerns: No gospel offered. Conscience decides; LCMS and WELS families are typically more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth toward a changed life in the second half; friends who reach out.
frames.concerns: No grace named; holiness churches would weigh the sexual content and suicide plan heavily, the UMC less so.

frames.aligns: Serious literary treatment of sin, shame and reconciliation in the line of Baudelaire and confessional fiction; judged by framing.
frames.concerns: Nihilism unanswered; content with minors. Practice ranges widely.

frames.aligns: The cost of secrecy and the value of confession and community; no violence made heroic.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes the explicitness a heavy concern; Old Order groups would avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Repentance and a changed life; family repair (Nakamura's mother).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; sexual content with minors, vulgar language and the suicide plan put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Compassion for outcasts (Nakamura); honest treatment of shame, consent and mental health; restoration over punishment.
frames.concerns: A boy's sexual assault is little addressed afterward (to verify); the suicide plan against safe-messaging norms. Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Hidden sin brings ruin; a later turn to a healthier life.
frames.concerns: No hope beyond human ties. Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the sexual content and despair a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Immorality and theft are shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: No hope in God's Kingdom; jw.org counsel on entertainment featuring immorality makes the sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Love and acceptance (Saeki, Tokiwa) help Kasuga out of self-condemnation.
frames.concerns: Shame, despair and the suicide plan dwelt on at length; members guard thought ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Teshuvah has an echo: confession, facing those he wronged, and a changed life. Choosing life over death at the festival.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the sexual content and language a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; dignity of the outcast; choosing life.
frames.concerns: Degrading sexual content involving minors and vulgar speech concern Jewish values of modesty and dignity.

frames.aligns: Honest about shame, coercion and mental health; repair of relationships.
frames.concerns: The suicide plan; sexual content with minors; Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Wrongdoing is exposed and leads to loss; later repentance-like change.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the voyeurism, underwear theft and sexual content a heavy concern; despair of mercy (Qur'an 39:53) is voiced and not answered in faith.

frames.aligns: Karma-like consequences from one act; the turn from tamasic confusion toward clarity and creative work.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content under Gita 17; views vary by community.
