frames.aligns: Close to teaching on craving, attachment and a constructed self: Kasuga's idealized self-image and idealized Saeki both fall apart ("I am an empty person"), and peace comes from acceptance.
frames.concerns: Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sexual and suicide scenes a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Lust, ego and attachment shown as destructive; humility and honest work later.
frames.concerns: Lust shown on the page is a depiction concern; no spiritual answer.

frames.aligns: Sexual wrongdoing and despair shown as damaging; reconciliation and service later.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" makes the sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) over false appearances is the story's core contrast; purification after a hometown "impurity" when Kasuga leaves and later returns. The festival is a matsuri (from general knowledge; to verify whether a shrine is shown).
frames.concerns: Disrupting a festival float is an act some families may weigh as disrespect toward a community and kami celebration.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility; harm shown as harm (the Rede). No witches or pagans stereotyped.
Survival chosen over death; honesty about one's own overts (wrong acts) and their effects.
frames.concerns: Depression framed as psychological; any push toward psychiatric help would run against the church's stance. No content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Serious treatment of shame, puberty and mental health; no glamorized fan service; the outcast given dignity.
frames.concerns: Voyeurism and theft of girls' underwear; a boy's sexual assault whose aftermath gets little attention (to verify); the suicide plan, which safe-messaging guidelines advise care with.

frames.aligns: This-life focus; self-knowledge, honesty, friendship and creative work as what makes life livable; critique of empty conformity without nihilism winning.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and the suicide plan are a depiction concern, Significant for minors.

frames.aligns: Shows where a loss of restraint leads; the later turn to responsibility, school and a steady relationship.
frames.concerns: Rebellion against family and community is voiced sympathetically; the good, the true and the beautiful are often degraded on the page.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of an outcast; honest search for meaning; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness makes it older-teen or adult reading.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against hypocrisy and conformity, with Baudelaire (who wrote "Litanies of Satan," from general knowledge; to verify) as the patron text; self-determination in the end.
frames.concerns: Coercion of others and a sexual assault go against the Eleven Rules' consent principles; the girls' stolen clothing is a violation of others.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Nakamura's attack on Kasuga's father (vol. 6) and Saeki's arson (vol. 5) are not celebrated; the later beach fight (vol. 11) ends in reconciliation, not victory.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The first arc celebrates breaking free of small-town conformity ("the other side of the mountain"); the festival plan is stopped (ch. 33) and the second arc values chosen, ordinary freedom.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families are distant and the school hushes the case (vol. 6); help comes from friends (Tokiwa, Kinoshita) more than kin, though Nakamura's mother offers her peace (vol. 10-11).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: No elder or leader is held up for deference; teachers and parents are marginal.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith or custom guides anyone; Baudelaire and literature take that place.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Finding one's true self and writing it (Tokiwa's novel, Kasuga's writing, vol. 8-11) is the story's resolution.

folkways.japan: The pressure to be "normal," the closed middle-school class, a school handling a scandal internally and a family moving away to escape shame (vol. 6) reflect Japanese norms of group harmony and face; the story criticizes these more than it endorses them.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise that "everything is established through the natural flow of the aesthetics and scenes, not by anything being told to us" (Creamer).
delivery.note: The series gives each of its three teenagers' views a sympathetic voice and lets consequences, not statements, carry its verdicts.

personified.ideology: Nihilistic contempt for conformity; escape to "the other side"
Literature and creative work as a way to live
Romantic self-image as a Baudelairean outsider

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (voiced, then moved past), Expressive individualism (explored), with secular humanism and a Dharmic echo in the recovery arc.

entry.heading: Homunculus
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The series does not hold up a model of a good life. It shows people hiding guilt and trauma behind masks (money, rank, surgery, lies), and asks whether a person who has no self underneath the mask can be healed at all. Its answer, as summaries read it, is bleak: Nakoshi's search for himself ends in self-mutilation, a woman's death and a world in which every face is his own.

frames.aligns: Lies, vanity and the refusal to know oneself lead to ruin; the kumicho's confession and act of reparation echo contrition and penance.
frames.concerns: Sexual use of a minor framed ambiguously; mutilation of the body (CCC 2297); no hope beyond the self; evil sometimes made fascinating, against Inter Mirifica 7. Sexual content and nudity are a heavy depiction concern (CCC 2521-2525).

frames.aligns: A study of the passions (vanity, lust, self-love) and a soul without a true face; their cost is shown.
frames.concerns: No repentance or grace in the tradition's sense; the self dissolves rather than being healed. Watchfulness over the senses (nepsis) makes the sexual imagery and body horror a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences (lies, lust, self-harm) are not hidden.
frames.concerns: No hope in Christ; a minor's sexual exploitation not clearly condemned; skull drilling as a path to "truth". Under Philippians 4:8 the sexual content, gore and suicide are a heavy concern. Congregations are self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: A picture of a fallen self that cannot remake itself; masks and lies exposed. Many in this tradition distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer; the Yukari scene; the series' open verdict. Explicitness is high even for families who "engage" culture.

frames.aligns: Shows a man opening himself to unseen forces and being destroyed by it.
frames.concerns: ESP and a "sixth sense" gained by drilling the skull may be read as an "open door"; no spiritual answer; sexual content. Holiness standards make it a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: The heart's deceitfulness (Jeremiah 17:9) has a strong echo: the homunculi may be Nakoshi's own projections. Common grace lets adults value serious art.
frames.concerns: No grace; the Yukari scene; self-mutilation. WLC Q139 makes the sexual imagery a heavy concern; suicide as self-murder (WLC Q136), treated pastorally.

frames.aligns: A man curved in on himself (incurvatus in se), shown to his ruin.
frames.concerns: No word of forgiveness. Conscience-based; LCMS and WELS families are typically far more cautious than ELCA about the content.

frames.aligns: The kumicho's turn from violence; Ito's reconciliation with his father.
frames.concerns: No grace named; sexual exploitation of a minor. Holiness churches avoid it; UMC families would see it as adult reading.

frames.aligns: Works judged by how they frame good and evil; the story shows vanity and lies destroying a man.
frames.concerns: The Yukari scene's framing; no hope offered. Content puts it firmly in adult literary reading.

frames.aligns: Violence leads to ruin; the yakuza boss leaves violence behind.
frames.concerns: A world with no community to catch anyone; mutilation and sexual content. Old Order groups would avoid it; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Repentance and restitution (the kumicho); a father-son reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Sexual exploitation of a minor; self-mutilation; no hope beyond the self. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; this falls outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Trauma taken seriously; a sympathetic arc for a gender-questioning character (Ito, per Looper); homelessness shown humanely.
frames.concerns: A minor's sexual exploitation framed ambiguously; women as objects of the hero's need; suicide shown.

frames.aligns: Unhealthy, self-destroying living shown as destroying.
frames.concerns: No hope; sexual content; body horror. "By beholding we become changed" and Fundamental Belief 22 make it a heavy concern; health teaching weighs the self-mutilation.

frames.aligns: Immorality and violence shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: Psychic "sixth sense" content may be weighed as spiritism; sexual immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); violence (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Nakoshi's visions may be his own thought; the story sees mind as shaping experience.
frames.concerns: Trauma, disease and mutilation presented as the deepest reality; surgery as the path to insight. "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392) makes dwelling on it a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: The body is not ours to damage; teshuvah echoed in the kumicho's confession.
frames.concerns: Self-wounding (chavalah); sexual exploitation of a minor; no moral verdict. Tzniut and nivul peh make it a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; the dignity of the homeless.
frames.concerns: Self-mutilation; the Yukari scene; no verdict. Degrading sexual content is a concern under modesty values.

frames.aligns: Harm to the vulnerable shown as harm; Ito's self-acceptance.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a minor framed ambiguously; women as objects.

frames.aligns: Lying and vanity lead to ruin; repentance (the kumicho).
frames.concerns: Changing God's creation (Qur'an 4:119, cited on cosmetic surgery) is a theme the story explores without a verdict; self-harm; sexual content with a minor. Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes it a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like return: each "cure" lands on Nakoshi's own body.
frames.concerns: No path to release; self-harm; sexual content. Tamasic content under Gita 17. Views vary.

frames.aligns: Close to teaching on no-self and clinging: Nakoshi grasps after a fixed self and ends trapped in a world of his own face; masks of ego; suffering born of craving.
frames.concerns: No path out of suffering; the ending is dissolution, not liberation. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sexual and gore content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, ego, attachment) shown as destructive; haumai (ego) as the root problem.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer; lust on the page.
Sexual content with a minor; no spiritual answer. The call to a "chaste and holy life" makes it a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and its absence: a man built on lies.
frames.concerns: Bodily impurity (kegare): blood, death and mutilation. No shrines or kami mocked.

frames.aligns: Self-knowledge as a theme; no witches or pagans stereotyped; "homunculus" as alchemical image.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none") is broken repeatedly, against Yukari and Nanako.

frames.aligns: Trauma images that bind a person until confronted echo the church's own teaching on past trauma (my own framing); survival of self.
frames.concerns: Ito's psychoanalytic and medical framing, and brain surgery as the path to insight, run against the church's stance on psychiatry and brain intervention.

frames.aligns: Sympathetic gender-identity arc for Ito (Looper; MAL review); trauma, homelessness and appearance culture taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Sexual activity between an adult and a 17-year-old framed as "rescue" rather than clearly as abuse; reviewers call it a rape scene; women as objects of the protagonist's need; suicide by hanging.

frames.aligns: Ito's skeptical, scientific frame; the placebo reveal; critique of pseudoscience (trepanation as insight) can be read in.
frames.concerns: Unethical human experiments are the premise and not clearly condemned; cruelty to the vulnerable.

frames.aligns: Shows the emptiness of a life of money, vanity and lies.
frames.concerns: No stable family, faith or duty offered; exploitation of a minor; mutilation. Content that degrades the good, true and beautiful.

frames.aligns: Free search for identity; Ito's self-acceptance; dignity of the homeless.
frames.concerns: The worth and dignity of Yukari and Nanako are violated; adult reading only.

frames.aligns: Self-determination and the rejection of social masks; skepticism toward the supernatural.
frames.concerns: Harm to a minor and unwanted sexual advances, which the Eleven Rules condemn, are framed ambiguously.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The yakuza code of finger-cutting is shown as guilt in disguise; the boss's last cut is atonement, not honor, and he leaves the gang (Japanese Wikipedia; JP v4-6 likely).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Institutions (hospital, gang, family) fail; Nakoshi lives outside all rules in his car; the story neither celebrates order nor endorses his freedom.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families harm (Ito's father, Yukari's parents) though Ito reconciles with his father; the homeless park is the nearest thing to community (Ita-san).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank (banker, doctor, yakuza boss) is shown as a mask over trauma; no elder is held up for deference.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; the frame is scientific and psychoanalytic (Ito's experiments, placebo reveal).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The story is about the self and its expression (surgery, identity, Ito's transition), set among the homeless struggling to survive.

folkways.japan: Yakuza finger-cutting (yubitsume), compensated dating and burusera shops, heavy education pressure, appearance culture and the homeless of Shinjuku are Japanese context the story uses as setting; it criticizes more than endorses them.

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers call it "overexplained and pretentious" and "pseudo-philosophical"; Ito explains psychoanalytic theory on the page.
delivery.note: Ideas about trauma and the self are spelled out in dialogue, but the story never settles whether Nakoshi's visions are real.

personified.ideology: Scientific skepticism about the mind and the occult
A self made of surface: money, surgery, lies

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Postmodernism (identity as surface), Naturalism, Nihilism (explored).

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 6: Stone Ocean
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Stone Ocean
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ストーンオーシャン

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 6: Stone Ocean
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen, not fated: loyalty to family and friends, courage under unjust power, and sacrifice for the weak are worth more than the peace of a destiny imposed from above, and hope in an unknown future is part of being human.

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): Pucci's scheme fails and his "Heaven" is shown as false. The story sides with free will against fate, close to CCC 1730-1742; Jolyne's death for Emporio echoes John 15:13. Concern for prisoners and the falsely accused echoes the works of mercy (Matthew 25:36). Pucci keeps a confession secret (ch. 127-129).
frames.concerns: A priest as the main villain who misuses Scripture (Christ "fated" to the cross, ch. 143) and gives God-like love to DIO (ch. 94). Fatalism differs from Providence, which works with free creatures (CCC 302-308). Masturbation reference (ch. 1), sexual subtext with a minor, gore; reincarnation-like ending (CCC 1013).

frames.aligns: Freedom (autexousion) and synergy over fate; a counterfeit "Heaven" exposed; self-sacrificial love.
frames.concerns: A cleric turned servant of a demonic figure; Christ's passion recast as blind fate (ch. 143); a universe remade without God; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs the gore and the sexual material.

frames.aligns: Evil is clearly framed as evil and defeated; a religious leader whose faith is false (Matthew 7:15-20); self-sacrifice; justice for the falsely accused.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: constant gore, a masturbation reference (ch. 1), sexual subtext, strong language. A priest-villain misusing Scripture. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Engaging culture: a story that rejects a counterfeit heaven built by a false shepherd and honors self-giving love (ch. 155). Depicts without endorsing.
frames.concerns: Pucci's "happiness" is peace without God; the story offers no gospel alternative, only human hope. Sexual material and gore (Romans 14 conscience).

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; a demonic figure's plan defeated.
frames.concerns: Souls pulled from bodies, a baby born from absorbed souls (ch. 76-77, 95), devotion to a vampire "as God" (ch. 94), "the 14 phrases" recited from DIO's notebook (ch. 95): many would see an "open door" to spiritual darkness.

frames.aligns: A rich talking point: Pucci's "gravity" is impersonal fatalism, while the Westminster Confession (3.1) says God's decree does no "violence... to the will of the creatures." Common grace lets families value the craft.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 on lascivious material (ch. 1, the DIO-Pucci flashback); gore; a pastor figure using Scripture to justify murder.

frames.aligns: Bondage of the will is about sin, not blind fate; the story sides with grace-like gifts (sacrifice, friendship). Vocation of a father (Jotaro).
frames.concerns: A priest villain; Christ's cross called "fate" (ch. 143) rather than a free self-giving; sexual material. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace and free response fit the story's rejection of fate; social holiness: the falsely imprisoned and abused.
frames.concerns: Gore, language, sexual material; holiness churches more cautious than UMC (General Rules on diversions).

frames.aligns: Imaginative fiction judged by framing (Lewis's tradition): a counterfeit heaven (compare The Great Divorce) defeated by love. Article 17 cautions against despair from a misused doctrine of predestination, which is Pucci's path.
frames.concerns: Clergy as villain; gore and sexual material.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a church official who serves another master; suffering of prisoners; Jolyne's sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' main tool, ending with Pucci beaten to death as he begs (ch. 158) (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Moral agency is central to the plan of salvation (2 Nephi 2:27), and the story defends agency against a forced, fore-known fate; family across generations; sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: the masturbation reference, sexual subtext and gore do not invite the Spirit for many families; a resetting universe.

frames.aligns: Critique of the carceral state and of racist violence (ch. 128); a female lead; a clergyman who abuses pastoral power is exposed.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; the slur in the manga; Anasui's femicide treated lightly as backstory.

frames.aligns: Free will and the great controversy between good and evil; a false "heaven" exposed.
frames.concerns: The state of the dead: souls taken out as discs, a ghost room, and the dead returning in a new universe conflict with Fundamental Belief 26; "by beholding we become changed" weighs the gore and sexual material.

frames.aligns: A religious leader who uses God's name for evil is condemned.
frames.concerns: Spiritism-like content (souls extracted, the dead returning), constant violence (Psalm 11:5), sexual material; jw.org counsel on entertainment weighs these heavily. Jesus is said to die on a "cross" (ch. 143).

frames.aligns: Fear is overcome; Pucci's "gravity" as a mental law resisted.
frames.concerns: Fear, decay and death shown as overwhelming and real; body horror; time and matter as all-powerful.

frames.aligns: "All is foreseen, yet freedom is given" (Avot 3:15) and Rambam on free will (Hilchot Teshuvah 5) fit the heroes' stand; racism and lynching condemned.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh: the masturbation reference, strip search, sexual subtext, language; gore. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Free will against fate; justice for the wrongly imprisoned; racism condemned.
frames.concerns: Sexual material and gore; Christian clergy as villain is not a Jewish concern in itself. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in the critique of prisons and racism; a woman as hero.
frames.concerns: Violence; the slur in the manga. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Pucci's love of DIO "as I love God" (ch. 94) is a form of shirk, and he is defeated; justice for the oppressed; mercy and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Qadar (divine decree) is a pillar of faith, but Pucci's version removes human responsibility; he says Jesus was put on the cross (ch. 143), which Qur'an 4:157-158 denies (said by a villain); lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the sexual material; gore.

frames.aligns: Cyclical time and a universe that ends and begins again echo the kalpas; karma: Pucci's actions return to him; the Gita's call to act rightly whatever the outcome (2.47).
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (gore, cruelty); the "reset" is achieved by a villain, not dharma.

frames.aligns: Craving and attachment drive Pucci; release from fear comes not from knowing the future but from compassion and right action; cycles of time.
frames.concerns: Non-harm (first precept) against constant killing; the final killing of a begging enemy.

frames.aligns: Hukam (divine order) is accepted in Sikh teaching, but through humility, not ego; Pucci shows haumai (ego) disguised as acceptance. Defending the weak.
frames.concerns: Violence and sexual material; a vision of the divine will imposed by force.

frames.aligns: Free will and the unity of humankind: racist violence (ch. 128) is shown as evil; a false religious leader is exposed.
frames.concerns: Constant violence; sexual material ("chaste and holy life").

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in the heroes; gratitude (Emporio's debt to Jolyne and Weather, ch. 157); renewal after the reset.
frames.concerns: Death, blood and corpses (kegare) are constant.

frames.aligns: Cycles of time and rebirth; a moon-timed ritual (the new moon at Cape Canaveral) framed as power, not evil in itself; the self-directed will.
Self-determinism against an imposed fate; personal responsibility. The Way to Happiness: "Do not murder."
frames.concerns: Memories and abilities ripped out as discs; constant killing by heroes and villains.

frames.aligns: First female JoJo, refusing an editor's request to make her male (Wikipedia); critique of the carceral state (Anime Feminist); racist violence condemned; a trans inmate shown respectfully (TV Tropes YMMV).
frames.concerns: Anasui's dismemberment of his girlfriend treated as quirky backstory while he courts Jolyne; the "queer" slur (manga); DIO-Pucci subtext with a 16-year-old; Anime Feminist notes Jolyne starts as "the least in control of her own power."

frames.aligns: Human choice and solidarity beat a cosmic plan; the religious villain's "Heaven" is false; hope without guarantees.
frames.concerns: The supernatural is central as fiction; heavy violence.

frames.aligns: Father-daughter love and duty (Jotaro, Jolyne); loyalty, sacrifice and courage; evil punished.
frames.concerns: A priest as villain; heroes are convicts; masturbation reference and sexual subtext; strong language.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth (prisoners, outsiders); free search for meaning; religion used for harm critiqued.
A religious authority who claims to know what is best for all humanity is defeated; individual will and self-determination win.
frames.concerns: Proportional retaliation (Church of Satan) and compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1) would read the final killing differently; the DIO-Pucci material involving a minor (Eleven Rules on children).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are settled personally, not by courts: Ermes's revenge for her sister (likely ch. 51-57), Weather's vow against Pucci (ch. 133-137), Emporio's debt (ch. 157). Courts are rigged (ch. 1-8).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Prison order is oppressive and the villain's ideal is total order of fate; freedom of choice is the story's prize.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Bloodline and father-daughter loyalty drive the plot (ch. 11, 75, 154); a found family of inmates; the civic institutions fail.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Guards' and the chaplain's authority are abused; a child, Emporio, wins.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious authority is the villain's; the heroes choose for themselves. A bloodline legacy remains honored.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in prison comes first; Jolyne's style and self-possession lean toward self-expression.

folkways.japan: The Joestar "bloodline" and inherited duty, and the gratitude and debt Emporio feels (on), reflect Japanese norms. A Catholic priest as a stylish villain fits a Japanese pop-culture habit of borrowing Christian imagery without Christian doctrine, which matches Araki's statement that the priesthood was only a facade. The idea of a universe that cycles and returns to its origin, which Araki named, has echoes in Buddhist ideas of time (from general knowledge; to verify; no source links Araki to it).

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls Pucci the franchise's most well-intentioned villain; ANN's writers say the story answers his fate with hope and choice.
delivery.note: The villain argues his theology of fate in long speeches, and the story answers him through the heroes' choices and sacrifices rather than counter-sermons.

personified.ideology: Accepting a known fate is happiness; God's will as irresistible "gravity"
Will and hope against fate; sacrifice for others
Choice and justice can change fate
Victim of racism and fate who answers with vengeance

entry.dominant: Existentialism (affirmed), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Collectivism/authoritarianism and Stoic-style fatalism (critiqued through Pucci), Christian (explored through a villain), Critical theory and Feminism (explored).

entry.title: Kagurabachi
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In modern Japan, years after a war fought with enchanted swords, a sorcerer gang kills the swordsmith Kunishige Rokuhira and steals six of his blades. His son Chihiro takes up the seventh blade to recover and destroy the stolen weapons, fighting yakuza-linked criminals and sorcerers along the way.
entry.life_message: A life of carrying a parent's legacy responsibly, protecting the vulnerable and facing the past honestly.

content.note: Frequent sword and sorcery killings, severed limbs and a mass-casualty attack (Wikipedia); AniList Gore tag 76%.
Murder of a parent, criminal auctions, wartime atrocities in backstory (Wikipedia; AniList Tragedy, Revenge tags).
No romance or sexual content noted in sources.
Some coarse language likely in gang scenes (to verify).
A character eats candy cigarettes; no real drug use noted.
Grief and survivor's guilt; a suicide in one character's backstory (Wikipedia) (to verify).
Revenge quest and armed vigilante action against criminals.
Popular Jump title with merchandise; no in-story product focus.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics; Might makes right (critiqued); Existentialism

frames.aligns: Filial devotion, protecting innocents and atonement for wartime wrongs.
frames.concerns: Revenge-driven plot and graphic killings; sorcery as power. Raised from C: gore is depiction.

frames.aligns: Grief for a father and costly self-giving for others.
frames.concerns: Vengeance and bloodshed sit uneasily with the call to repentance for killing.

frames.aligns: Protecting the weak and opposing organized crime.
frames.concerns: Revenge motive (Romans 12:19), gore and sorcery would prompt caution.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty and a hero who restrains his worst impulses.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence and magic-based powers worth discussing with teens.

frames.aligns: Clear struggle between protector and predators.
frames.concerns: Sorcery, cursed powers and a Shinto goddess-linked ability touch spiritual-warfare concerns.

frames.aligns: Shows sin's long consequences, judged through common grace.
frames.concerns: Personal vengeance and sorcery; graphic deaths.

frames.aligns: Lawful order against criminal gangs; vocation of a craftsman.
frames.concerns: Vigilante action outside lawful authority; violence and magic.

frames.aligns: Mercy toward victims and a hero tempted but not ruled by hatred.
frames.concerns: Revenge and bloodshed weigh against a peace emphasis; protection is the frame.

frames.aligns: Moral seriousness about war guilt and justice.
frames.concerns: Revenge framing and gore judged case by case.

frames.aligns: Remorse over war and its weapons; destroying instruments of death.
frames.concerns: Sword violence as the hero's path conflicts with nonresistance.

frames.aligns: Honoring a father and defending the innocent.
frames.concerns: Violent content the youth guidance cautions against; sorcery themes. Raised from C.

frames.aligns: Critiques war crimes and weapons that kill civilians.
frames.concerns: Glorified sword combat and revenge may concern a peace-and-justice view.

frames.aligns: Justice against oppressors and loyalty to family.
frames.concerns: Sorcery (sihr) as central power; revenge over forgiveness; gore.

frames.aligns: Duty to family and righteous fight against wrongdoers.
frames.concerns: Ahimsa concerns over graphic violence; occult sorcery.

frames.aligns: Shows how violence and vengeance breed further suffering.
frames.concerns: Heavy killing tests the first precept; the story shows its cost.

frames.aligns: Critiques war atrocities and criminal exploitation.
Responsibility for consequences of technology and war.
frames.concerns: Gore and revenge; supernatural powers as fiction.

frames.aligns: Filial loyalty, craftsmanship and heroism against criminals.
Honoring a father; destroying weapons of war.
Opposing criminals who traffic in people.
frames.concerns: Sorcery, gore and revenge combat Witnesses avoid.
Dismemberment and death imagery dwell on fear.

frames.aligns: Accountability for war atrocities; protecting victims of trafficking.
Rede-like restraint: Chihiro limits the harm he does.
frames.concerns: Sorcerers shown as criminal gangs, a negative stereotype of magic users.

frames.aligns: Swordsmith craft and a goddess-linked blade echo shrine traditions.
Defending the oppressed with a sword, close to the saint-soldier ideal.
frames.concerns: Revenge as motive; sorcery treated as real.

frames.aligns: Justice and an end to weapons of war.
Taking responsibility for one's legacy and actions.
Justice pursued against predators without waiting on authority.
Honoring a parent and seeking justice against killers.
frames.concerns: Revenge (lo tikom); sorcery as power source; gore.

frames.aligns: Honoring a parent; justice for the murdered.
Accountability for war and protecting trafficking victims.

delivery.evidence: ANN guide reviewers note Chihiro is driven by anger, revenge the audience can understand; none call it preachy

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Martial pride and the tournament code of honor run through the series; Vegeta's bloodline pride drives his arc. The story also honors mercy (sparing Frieza) and Vegeta's turn from pride to self-sacrifice (ch. 467).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Goku fights for the joy of it and does not seek command; each arc's hero is stronger but chooses not to rule (Philosophy essay). Gods are bureaucrats and mentors, not lawgivers, and Goku leaves home to train Uub (ch. 517-519).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Goku protects Earth because his friends live there. Former enemies join the circle (Piccolo, Vegeta, Buu). Family is present but often secondary to friends and training.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Tyrants who want to own others are destroyed (Frieza, Cell, Kid Buu). Rank exists among fighters and gods (Kais, Supreme Kai), but strength is earned by training, and rivals are welcomed as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A Buddhist, Taoist and folk cosmology (King Yama, Kami, halos) is setting, not worship; Toriyama said he did not think deeply about it. Capsule Corp technology and whatever works solve problems (Pragmatic lens).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Joyful striving is the life message: train, enjoy the fight, food and friends. Death is often reversible through the Dragon Balls, so security fears weigh lightly.

folkways.japan: The Jump formula of friendship, effort and victory, the master-and-disciple training model (Roshi, Kami) and the folk cosmology borrowed from Chinese and Japanese Buddhism reflect Japanese boys' manga norms of the 1980s and 1990s rather than the story's own argument.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Values of effort and friendship come through comedy and fights with little direct moral commentary.

entry.title: Innocent

entry.premise: A historical drama loosely based on the real Sanson family, hereditary executioners of Paris before the French Revolution. Gentle Charles-Henri Sanson recoils from the killing his inherited office demands but accepts it to protect his family, vowing to be the last executioner. His younger sister Marie-Joseph rebels against the gender rules of her time and seeks a place in the executions and at court.
entry.life_message: It holds up refusing to let birth, office or society dictate who you are, even at great personal cost.

content.note: Graphic executions with heavy blood, a father torturing his son by breaking his legs, and animal cruelty (ANN reviews; Manga Critic; AniList Gore 81%, Torture 79%).

entry.title: Gin Tama
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In an alternate Edo-era Japan conquered by aliens called Amanto, swords are banned and the samurai class has collapsed. Former rebel samurai Gintoki Sakata runs an odd-jobs business, the Yorozuya, with teenager Shinpachi and the super-strong alien girl Kagura. A young Priestess's first adventuring party is destroyed by goblins, and she is rescued by Goblin Slayer, a silver-ranked adventurer who survived a goblin massacre of his village as a child and now does nothing but hunt goblins. entry.title: Mission: Yozakura Family

entry.premise: Taiyo Asano, a shy high schooler who lost his family in a car crash, learns that his childhood friend Mutsumi heads a clan of elite spies. entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Akiko Higashimura's autobiographical manga follows her from a cocky high-school student who wants to be a manga artist to a working professional. Her rural art teacher, Kenzou Hidaka, is harsh, temperamental and swings a bamboo sword, yet he pours himself into her training. Looking back as an adult, Akiko weighs how she drifted from his lessons and what she owes him.
entry.life_message: A good life is built by daily, honest work at your craft and by honoring the teachers who believed in you before it is too late.

content.note: Teacher wields a bamboo sword at students, played for comedy (AniList blurb, Swordplay tag) (to verify).

entry.title: Zatch Bell!
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Arrogant, isolated genius Kiyo Takamine receives a strange boy named Zatch Bell from his father, who hopes it will help him make friends. Zatch is one of 100 mamodo children sent to the human world to fight for the throne of their world, each partnered with a human who reads spells from their book. Kiyo and Zatch battle other pairs, make allies, and resolve to make Zatch a 'kind king'.
entry.life_message: True strength is kindness: a ruler and a friend should protect others and grow through loyalty, not domination.

entry.title: Love Hina

entry.premise: Keitaro Urashima has failed the Tokyo University entrance exam twice and is kicked out by his parents. His grandmother's Hinata inn turns out to be a girls' dormitory, and he becomes its manager among its female residents. He keeps studying for Todai, partly to keep a childhood promise to a girl he can't remember, while a chaotic romance builds among the residents (MU Love Polygon).

entry.title: Spice & Wolf
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In a medieval-Europe-like world, traveling merchant Kraft Lawrence finds Holo, a centuries-old wolf harvest deity in the form of a girl, hiding in his wagon. Feeling forgotten by farmers who no longer need her blessing, she travels with him toward her northern homeland. Her wit helps his trading schemes, the Church takes an unwelcome interest in her, and the two slowly fall in love.
entry.life_message: A good life is a shared journey of wit, honest bargaining and companionship that outlasts loneliness.

There his 'unlimited gacha' gift summons overwhelmingly powerful allies, led by the maid Mei. After finding his hometown massacred and humans enslaved by other races, he spends years building an underground base and sets out for revenge on his former party and on the races that oppress humanity.

entry.title: Sanctuary
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Akira Hojo and Chiaki Asami survived the Cambodian killing fields as boys and vowed to remake Japan as their 'sanctuary'. Choosing roles by rock-paper-scissors, Hojo rises through the yakuza to unite the syndicates while Asami fights aging politicians to reach the Diet and become prime minister. Both use ruthless, often criminal means, and the series ends with their return to Cambodia and Asami's death from illness.
entry.life_message: Bold young men willing to use any means, legal or not, can break a stagnant order and remake their nation.

He hides his level and travels the world as a merchant and sightseer, gathering a party of rescued slave girls, an elf and a homunculus. Manga adaptation of a web-born light novel.
entry.life_message: A good life is a calm one: travel, good food and quietly using great power to look after the people who join you.

entry.title: Franken Fran
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Fran, an artificial girl built by the vanished surgeon Dr. Madaraki, carries on his medical work at a remote mansion in rural Japan. Patients come to her for cosmetic surgery, strength, popularity or even resurrection, and her radical operations keep them alive but often leave them grotesquely mutated. The episodic chapters are 'monkey's paw' stories that use body horror and black comedy to satirize the obsessions that drive people to her.
entry.life_message: Life itself is to be preserved at any cost, while the story's satire suggests that vanity and greed bring their own monstrous results.

entry.premise: Natsuo Ishido, a high school first-year who is effortlessly good at every sport, is bored, lonely and openly contemptuous of opponents. After a bloody spar with Yuzuko Mawatari, the untalented but relentless captain of a new mixed martial arts club, she quits volleyball to train in MMA so she can beat her. entry.premise: In an alternate Taisho-era Japan where spirits and inherited supernatural gifts exist, Miyo Saimori, born without powers, is treated as a servant by her stepmother, half-sister and indifferent father. She is sent as a bride candidate to Kiyoka Kudo, a military commander rumored to be so cold that earlier fiancees fled within days. entry.title: Sleepy Princess in the Demon Castle
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Princess Syalis has been kidnapped by the Demon King and held in his castle while a hero sets out to rescue her. Bored and unable to sleep well, she ignores the danger and devotes herself to getting comfortable, raiding the castle for bedding, such as fur from her teddy-bear demon guards and a magical shield turned air mattress. Her schemes often end in her own accidental death or the deaths of minor demons, undone by the castle's demon cleric, and she comes to treat the castle as home while her clumsy hero-fiance fails to arrive (Wikipedia; VIZ blurbs; AniList Slapstick, Episodic).
entry.life_message: Rest and comfort are worth pursuing, and even 'enemies' can become a kind of household.

entry.premise: Yukino Miyazawa keeps up a perfect-student facade to win praise, until rival Soichiro Arima tops the class, discovers her real self and the two fall in love, vowing to drop their fake ways. As friends gather around them, the story turns darker: Arima's own perfection hides fear of becoming like the parents who abandoned him, and the return of his abusive mother and absent father drives him into a crisis. entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Orphaned high schooler Ataru Kashiwagi lives in poverty with his younger sister Yuri and finds refuge in friends on the social network Real Account. He and about 10,000 users are pulled into a virtual version of the app, where the mascot Marble forces them into deadly games: a player who loses all followers dies, and when a player dies, so do their followers, while the world watches. entry.premise: Middle schoolers Kanata Tanaka and Kazuki Yoshikawa, childhood friends seen by classmates as unusually mature, are drawn to each other but unsure how to act on it. The quiet, nostalgic story follows their secret first romance through school days and festivals, with side stories about classmates, including one student's storyline with a music teacher.

entry.title: 5 Centimeters Per Second
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Yukiko Seike's manga adaptation of Makoto Shinkai's 2007 film follows Takaki Tono from childhood into adulthood. He and his close friend Akari are separated when her family moves, and their letters slowly thin out; later, classmate Kanae loves Takaki without being able to tell him. The manga extends the story, showing Kanae working as a nurse after the film's events.
entry.life_message: Time and distance change people, and growing up means learning to carry first love as memory and move on.

entry.premise: Reincarnated in another world as Astaroth, the 72nd and weakest demon king, a man from our world sets out to unite the land under his rule. Using knowledge from his past life, he applies cold strategy: striking heroes before they grow strong, wrecking enemy economies with counterfeit money and modernizing his forces. entry.title: Drifting Dragons
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In a world where dragons fly the skies like whales, the airship Quin Zaza is one of the last dragon-hunting ('draking') vessels. Its crew, including the skilled, reckless gourmet Mika and rookie Takita, hunt dragons for meat and materials, cook what they catch, and cope with repairs, money troubles and social isolation. Ostracized on the ground, the drakers depend on each other as a family.

entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: College student Hana falls in love with a man who is secretly a wolf in human form, and they have two children, Yuki and Ame, who can switch between human and wolf shape. entry.title: Buddha
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Osamu Tezuka's retelling of the life of Siddhartha, from sickly prince to wandering ascetic to enlightened teacher, set in a turbulent ancient India of wars, bandits and caste oppression. Invented characters such as the animal-possessing bandit Tatta, the slave-caste woman Migaila and the wolf-raised Devadatta surround the historical story. Tezuka, described by his publisher as a humanist rather than a Buddhist, mixes philosophy with action, slapstick and anachronistic jokes. Eisner Award winner; eight volumes in English.
entry.life_message: Enlightenment comes from seeing that all life is connected and answering suffering with compassion rather than revenge.

entry.title: Kobato.
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Kobato, a kind but naive girl with no memory of her past, must fill a magic bottle with the pain of hearts she has healed before four seasons pass so she can reach a place she longs to go. entry.title: Angel Sanctuary

entry.premise: Setsuna, a troubled 16-year-old, is in love with his 15-year-old sister Sara and learns he is the reincarnation of Alexiel, an angel who rebelled against Heaven. entry.title: Ayako
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In occupied post-war Japan, the landowning Tenge family loses its estates to land reform. When young Ayako witnesses secret murders by an elder brother who works as an agent for the US occupiers, the family locks her in an underground cellar to hide that crime and its own incestuous secrets; she stays there for over two decades while the country changes above her. entry.heading: Tokyo Ghoul
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Identity is a choice made under pressure: a person who belongs to two worlds can try to protect both, but the story counts the cost of that choice in pain and loss, and offers only a fragile hope that the two sides might one day live together.

content.framing: Neutral; predatory desire shown as menacing

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person, even the "monster"; critique of dehumanizing the outsider; evil (torture, revenge) shown as evil with consequences.
frames.concerns: Despair rather than hope dominates the original ending; revenge is pursued by several sympathetic characters; gratuitous gore in media is criticized by the Church ("Ethics in Communications").

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions (hunger as a picture of a consuming passion); compassion for the enemy.
frames.concerns: Darkness without theosis or grace; strong concern about images that feed the passions; the church setting used for a cannibal scene (vol. 4-5) touches reverence for holy places.

frames.aligns: Clear depiction of sin's consequences; friendship and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: No saving answer, only human striving; graphic violence and strong language (Ephesians 4:29). Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles writers read Kaneki's arc as a search for redemption: "to be human means to feel pain." Evil framed as evil; mercy toward outsiders.
frames.concerns: The redemption remains unfinished; occasional nihilistic voices; gore and language.

frames.aligns: Clear battle between destructive and protective power.
frames.concerns: Ghouls are not demons, but the predatory, possession-like imagery (Rize "inside" Kaneki's mind, ch. 62-63, likely) can concern families attentive to spiritual warfare.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed: every faction, human and ghoul, is capable of atrocity; common grace lets families value a serious work by a non-Christian author.
frames.concerns: No providence or grace in view; vengeance taken into human hands (WLC on the sixth commandment).

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: the story shows people unable to save themselves. Two kingdoms: questions about the state's use of force.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer offered; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: concern for the outcast and the hunted; works of mercy (Anteiku feeding ghouls without killing).
frames.concerns: No grace named, and the hope of coexistence is left unfinished. Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus" makes the graphic content a heavy depiction concern for holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan), less for many UMC families.

frames.aligns: Respect for the outsider; just-war questions (Article 37) about the CCG's campaign.
frames.concerns: Despair at the end; revenge cycles. Episcopal and ACNA families differ more on gender than on this content.

frames.aligns: The cycle of violence is shown as destroying everyone; Anteiku's nonviolent ethic and Kaneki's mother's "better to be hurt" echo nonresistance.
frames.concerns: Kaneki abandons that ethic and the story makes his violence effective. Conservative groups avoid such media entirely; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and the struggle of a divided nature; family love; service.
frames.concerns: A bleak ending with no hope beyond human effort; revenge pursued by sympathetic characters. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the gore and language are the depiction issue. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Concern for the outcast; consequences of evil; the body treated as something that matters.
frames.concerns: Adventist teaching on media (drawn from Ellen G. White and the church's guidelines) warns against entertainment that dwells on violence and horror; the cannibal premise also clashes with the health message. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Prejudice shown as wrong; peace preferred to violence.
frames.concerns: Witness publications (Watchtower, jw.org guidance on entertainment) counsel avoiding media that features violence (Psalm 11:5); fighting is the main way the story's conflicts are settled, though it is framed as tragedy, and the horror imagery is a heavy depiction concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge spreads harm: Mado's zeal and Touka's attacks (ch. 13-29) and Yamori repeating his own abuse (ch. 59-66). Kaneki's hardening to protect friends brings him no peace (ch. 80-94).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Authority on both sides, the CCG and Aogiri, uses violence as policy and is critiqued. Anteiku's quiet restraint, outside both systems, is the endorsed path.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family and protecting one's group come first (Anteiku, the Kirishima siblings, Hinami). Hide's friendship regardless of what Kaneki is, and the hope of coexistence, widen the circle.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A hidden minority hunted by an organized majority; prejudice and state violence are critiqued. Aogiri's "strong eat the weak" creed is shown as hollow.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Christian imagery recurs ("Original Sin," ch. 126; the church fight, vol. 4-5) but is symbolic and offers no rescue. Kanou's lab science is shown as horror (ch. 95-111), so neither pole is celebrated.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival dominates a world of constant death, but the story's central value is tolerance across groups and the choice of one's own identity (life message).

folkways.japan: Ishida's sense of being "between the majority and minority groups" speaks to conformity pressure in Japanese society; Kaneki's mother's ethic, "better to be hurt than to hurt others," echoes Japanese ideals of self-effacement that the story tests and then breaks.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Silverman notes Kaneki's ruthlessness "doesn't look like it has brought him any more happiness"; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The story presents both ghouls and the CCG from the inside and lets events, not narration, weigh their views.

entry.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story shows a life spent claiming the power to judge others, and lets the reader watch where that leads. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

content.frequency: Constant (deaths every few chapters), mostly non-graphic

frames.aligns: The ruin of a proud man who makes himself judge of life and death; the innocent suffer from his "justice"; lawful authority prevails. Evil is shown in order to be understood, not made finally attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: No repentance or grace; the "Mu" rule denies judgment and afterlife; Light's glamor can invite admiration. Coerced suicides and death gods weigh as depiction; many parishes would treat it as older-teen reading.

frames.aligns: Light as a picture of the passions, above all pride, and of a man refusing repentance; an Orthodox writer at Geeks Under Grace reads it as "the throne without the Cross."
frames.concerns: No hope of resurrection in the story's rules; death gods taken seriously as spirits; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on the long dwelling with a killer's mind.

frames.aligns: Clear arc from sin to ruin (Galatians 6:7); deception exposed; a thoughtful teen can discuss justice and the death penalty.
frames.concerns: A human claiming divinity is punished, but no gospel answer is given; the "Mu" ending; death gods. Profanity in the Viz text and coerced suicide fail many families' Philippians 4:8 test. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Plugged In praises the "compelling plot" and "conversations on morality and justice"; Christian reviewers read Light as a man seizing God's throne and falling.
frames.concerns: Plugged In warns of "spiritual themes, violence, and language" and apple and Eden imagery (anime). Range is broad, from churches that skip it to churches that use it for worldview talks.

frames.aligns: The man who takes a death god's power is destroyed by it.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a supernatural death god who gives a human power to kill, and a notebook that works like a curse, are shown without any power of God against them.

frames.aligns: Light as a study in total depravity: a gifted, "good" student whose heart turns to self-worship; through common grace, a non-Christian story tells the truth about sin and the magistrate's sword.
frames.concerns: No grace or providence named; constant lying by the protagonist; coerced suicides (self-murder, WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: God works through lawful authority (police, courts), and Light usurps it; the law exposes him in the end.
frames.concerns: The story shows law and judgment but no gospel. LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: "Do no harm" set against a man who does harm for "good"; Soichiro's integrity.
frames.concerns: Light refuses every chance to turn back, and the story offers none; profanity; holiness churches stricter than the UMC.

frames.aligns: Moral crime fiction in the Sayers tradition, judged by how it frames good and evil; lawful authority (Article 37) frames the duel.
frames.concerns: The nihilist "Mu" close; Light's glamor. ACNA families may be more cautious than Episcopal families.

frames.aligns: Violence and the will to punish shown as a trap that consumes the one who uses it; a critique of the death penalty.
frames.concerns: The heroes also use deception, confinement and guns; no peaceful alternative is shown. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families may read it as a critique of capital punishment.

frames.aligns: Agency and its consequences; honesty (Article of Faith 13) as what finally defeats a liar.
frames.concerns: The "Mu" rule against the plan of salvation; no repentance. Coerced suicide, profanity and the body count weigh against media that invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Pride and self-made godhood brought to ruin; deception exposed.
frames.concerns: Death gods and a spirit realm (spiritualism is strongly rejected); the "Mu" rule shares the teaching that the dead are unconscious but denies resurrection. Ellen White's caution about fiction that excites the passions. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Human attempts to rule and judge end in ruin; no hellfire (Ryuk: "no heaven or hell").
frames.concerns: Death gods as real spirits granting power (spiritism, a major concern in jw.org counsel); death as final with no resurrection hope; violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Truth exposes error; the deceiver's power proves empty.
frames.concerns: Death presented as real and final, against the teaching that life is spiritual; long dwelling on fear and death as mental influences. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: A sharp critique of the death penalty, vigilantism, surveillance and populist media fits the peace-and-justice focus.
frames.concerns: Women defined by love for Light (AnimeFeminist); suicides without mental-health framing.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and due process; the danger of a man who makes himself an idol, brought down.
frames.concerns: Taking life outside lawful courts is never redeemed; a human claiming godhood. Coerced suicide and death gods; Haredi homes would avoid it. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Private judgment and killing are the story's target: Light's vigilante "justice" ends in exposure and death (ch. 103-107). Soichiro and the task force, who stand for rule of law, duty and honesty, are the moral center.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Law and due process are endorsed over one man's will. L's surveillance and confinement of suspects (Misa, ch. 33-35) are questioned, so order is honored but not without limits.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Rules are meant to apply to all, including family: Soichiro serves the investigation even as it points at his son. Light risks his father and sister (vols. 7-9), a betrayal of kin the story condemns as part of his corruption.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Light's claim to be "god of the new world" (ch. 1-2) is the root wrong; no person is above the law. The police chain of command and the Wammy's House succession (Near, Mello) are shown neutrally.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious language belongs to the villain and his cult (Mikami, ch. 83; the Kira worshippers, ch. 108). The "Mu" rule offers a naturalist note, and the duel is won by reason and investigation.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Crime, safety and deterrence are the central question; a frightened public accepts a killer who promises security (Pragmatic lens). Ohba's takeaway, "let's give it our all while we're alive," adds a modest self-expression note.

folkways.japan: Capital punishment, a powerful police bureaucracy and the public's quiet approval of Kira reflect debates in Japan, which keeps the death penalty; scholar Jolyon Baraka Thomas reads the cult elements against the 1995 Tokyo sarin attack. Soichiro's quiet devotion to duty echoes Japanese workplace norms.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Briana Lawrence: "two opposing sides that both believe in the same thing: justice." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Light and L argue openly about justice, and the story ends with Light's fall rather than a stated lesson.

personified.ideology: Justice by results; one genius may judge and kill

entry.heading: Black Clover
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is earned by effort, not birth: you refuse to give up, you lift up the people others look down on, and you build a family out of misfits.

frames.aligns: Dignity of the poor and the orphan; a church that shelters children; evil (the Dark Triad, Lucius) is never made attractive in the end (Inter Mirifica 7); reconciliation with enemies.
frames.concerns: The hero's power comes from a devil shown as a friend; angels and "holy war" imagery belong to the villain; a consecrated nun is the object of a running marriage-proposal gag.

frames.aligns: Humility and endurance; love for enemies; a church that raises orphans.
frames.concerns: Demons are real in the tradition, so a demon made sympathetic and fused with the hero (Devil Union, ch. 272-273, 326-327) blurs the line; angelic forms (halos, wings) given to the villain's creations. Guarding the senses (nepsis) applies to the steady combat.

frames.aligns: Hard work, perseverance, care for the outcast (James 2:1-9 on favoritism to the rich).
frames.concerns: Magic and devil power as the hero's tools; views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; underdog grace; forgiveness of former enemies.
frames.concerns: The hero befriends and unites with a devil; spiritual realities in the story are not Christian ones. Engage-or-separate views differ.

frames.aligns: Courage, perseverance and a church shown kindly.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": devil contracts and hosting are the main source of power for heroes and villains alike, and the hero's union with a devil is celebrated (ch. 270, 326-327). Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians; human pride and lust for power (Lucius, the Dark Triad) shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: Devil alliance as the hero's strength; WLC Q139 concern for the fan service; images of angels and "holy war."

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: Magic Knights bear the sword to protect the weak; vocation and faithful service in ordinary roles.
frames.concerns: Devil power and magic; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: lifting up the poor and the excluded; works of mercy; prevenient grace has an echo in former enemies who turn.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules caution about diversions; the devil alliance; drinking played for laughs. Holiness churches usually more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Works judged by how they frame good and evil, in a fantasy tradition (Lewis; Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings is among Tabata's named influences, per Wikipedia); justice for the excluded.
frames.concerns: The devil alliance and inverted angel imagery; the nun gag. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender, not on this content.

frames.aligns: Care for outsiders, community of misfits, forgiveness of enemies.
frames.concerns: Heroic violence is the hero's main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); Old Order groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and effort; family (including adoptive family); service in a squad.
frames.concerns: Devil power and occult-style magic; fan service and drinking. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Strong critique of class, birth and ethnic prejudice; the excluded become heroes; a church that shelters children.
frames.concerns: The nun gag and early thin female cast (Anime Feminist; Fandom); violence as the means.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, care for orphans, clear defeat of devils.
frames.concerns: Magic, witches and devil hosting throughout; the dead brought back as Paladins conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: Kindness to the poor, loyalty, hard work.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and magic are the basis of the whole world, and the hero's power comes from a demon (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting is the hero's calling (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Persistence, hope and love outlasting hatred.
frames.concerns: Evil, devils and fear are shown as real powers; magic as the source of strength.

frames.aligns: Care for the orphan and stranger (Deuteronomy 10:18-19); honoring those who raised you; persistence.
frames.concerns: Magic (kishuf) and demon alliances are central; Kabbalistic terms (Qliphoth, Sephira) used as fantasy labels; tzniut concerns with outfits and gags. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Love of the stranger, social justice, reconciliation after historic wrong (the elves).
frames.concerns: Magic and demons; Kabbalistic terms as fantasy; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: dismantling prejudice by birth and nation; outsiders included; historic injustice remembered and repaired.
frames.concerns: Kabbalistic terms used loosely; violence as the main tool.

frames.aligns: Justice for the poor, the orphan and the stranger; patience (sabr) and effort; family loyalty.
frames.concerns: Magic (sihr) is central; the hero allies with a devil (shaytan) and fuses with it; angelic imagery used by the villain. Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for outfits and gags.

frames.aligns: Effort and duty; a warrior who fights without hatred; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the fighting; the birth-and-rank hierarchy story invites discussion that families approach in different ways.

frames.aligns: Compassion for outcasts and former enemies; Licht's hatred shown as suffering; craving for power (Lucius, Dark Triad) leads to ruin.
frames.concerns: Fighting is the main solution, against the first precept; ambition for the top rank is celebrated.

frames.aligns: Rejection of caste and birth-rank is a core Sikh value; courage to defend the oppressed; the five vices (ego, anger, greed) in the villains are condemned.
frames.concerns: Magic and devil power as a fantasy device; fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: Elimination of prejudice of every kind (race, class, nation) and the unity of peoples, as elves, humans and kingdoms are reconciled.
frames.concerns: Constant fighting; drinking played for laughs (alcohol is forbidden to Bahá'ís).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; the Hino Country and the Ryuzen clan draw on Japanese setting.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; devils are a Western-style underworld rather than kami or yokai.

frames.aligns: Magic as part of nature; spirits of the elements (Undine, Sylph) aid the heroes; Vanessa, a witch, is a sympathetic hero.
frames.concerns: The Witch Queen is a manipulative ruler (likely ch. 90s; to verify); a stereotype check for "witch" villains.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be industrious, do not murder; self-determinism in Asta.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; Lucius rewriting souls and minds is condemned, which fits the Church's concern about mind control.

frames.aligns: Anti-discrimination by class, ethnicity and ability is the core theme; disability-like "no magic" hero succeeds.
frames.concerns: The Sister Lily gag (Anime Feminist: a "refusal to respect a woman's wishes"; Fandom: "a kind of stalker"); fan service; Common Sense Media rates diverse representation "very little."

frames.aligns: Worth earned by effort and character, not birth or bloodline; human solidarity across peoples; magic read as fiction.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main tool; revivals lessen the weight of death.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-reliance, loyalty, duty, protecting the weak, respect for good mentors and a legitimate elected leader.
frames.concerns: Inherited aristocracy is critiqued; blood family often fails while found family succeeds; some religious conservatives raise the devil alliance.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person regardless of birth or power; justice for the excluded; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Violence as the means; the nun gag.

frames.aligns: A devil reframed as a misunderstood outcast; defiance of unjust authority and false holiness (Lucius's "Archangels"); self-reliance; Satanic Temple tenets on compassion and justice.
frames.concerns: Most devils are still villains, so the stereotype check applies; loyalty and self-sacrifice for the group over the self.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Asta answers insults by proving himself, not by revenge; rivalry is a matter of pride, but vendetta (Licht's, the elves') is shown as manipulated and is reconciled (ch. 214).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The chaotic, rule-bending Black Bulls are celebrated (ANN: "the magical misfits"), but the Magic Knights and the elected Wizard King are upheld (ch. 392).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family over blood: an orphanage and a squad, while Noelle's blood family is cruel (ch. 5). Protecting the whole kingdom, and later former enemies, is the goal.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank by birth and magic is the main target (Noble, Common and Forsaken realms); merit, not lineage, earns rank. The story still celebrates reaching the top rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The church is warm, but faith does not guide the plot; inherited aristocracy is critiqued; magic works like a natural force.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work and endurance drive the hero (survival), joined to tolerance of outsiders and being oneself (expression).

folkways.japan: Senpai-style mentoring by captains, group loyalty to a squad and hard-work ("ganbaru") perseverance are common Japanese shonen norms. The church, nuns and the European-fantasy kingdom are borrowed Western settings, and the Hino Country (Yami's home) is a Japan-like land seen from outside.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness. Trujillo (ANN) highlights its anti-discrimination themes.
delivery.note: Asta and his allies state the never-give-up and anti-discrimination themes aloud, while some snobbish rivals are later partly redeemed.

personified.ideology: Effort and loyalty can beat birth

entry.premise: A seinen comedy-drama by Hiroaki Samura set in Sapporo. Minare Koda, a heavy drinker, rants about her breakup to a stranger at a bar who turns out to be a radio producer; her recorded rant airs the next day, she storms the station, and she is talked into doing a show, discovering a talent for radio (Kodansha blurb; ANN Spring 2020 Manga Guide). Database tags list a cult storyline and an earthquake (AniList, MangaUpdates).
entry.life_message: A loud, messy person can find a voice and a vocation by throwing herself into the work in front of her.

content.note: Minare breaks down station doors (ANN); no serious violence indicated.
Earthquake and cult tags (MangaUpdates; AniList spoiler) (to verify).
A boss's sexual harassment of male staff played as a joke (ANN, Hopper); breakups (MangaUpdates).
Minare's 'acid tongue' (Kodansha) and 'hollering' (ANN); profanity level to verify.
Heavy drinking drives the plot (ANN); Alcohol and Smoking tags (MangaUpdates).
Heartbreak and frustration (blurb).
Producer uses a release she signed while drunk, 'skirting the lines of legality' (ANN).
Radio industry setting; anime adaptation.

entry.dominant: Finding a voice; workplace comedy; adult messiness

frames.concerns: Drunkenness central; consent and harassment treated lightly (ANN).

frames.aligns: Hard work at a new vocation.
frames.concerns: Heavy drinking, profanity, harassment as a joke.
Alcohol and smoking central (Word of Wisdom).
Harassment and drunken consent framed as jokes (ANN).
Fifth precept: drinking central; harsh speech.
Consent and harassment not challenged (ANN, Hopper).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Minare storms the station over the broadcast (Kodansha).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Unruly, impulsive heroine (ANN).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Coworkers and listeners, not family (blurb).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Producer manipulates; workplace pressure (ANN).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular modern media world.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression on air is the arc (blurb).

folkways.japan: Reflects Japanese seinen slice-of-life and regional Hokkaido settings, and workplace pressure where juniors are pushed into roles by superiors.

delivery.evidence: ANN reviewer Hopper says the book lacks clear moral framing of misconduct.
delivery.note: Behavior is shown without commentary, which one reviewer criticized.

entry.winners_losers: Minare wins an audience; reviewers note others' misconduct goes unchallenged.
to_verify: Cult storyline (spoiler tag) and earthquake arc.
Profanity level; only volume 1 reviewed.
Ongoing series.
