entry.heading: Naruto (Masashi Kishimoto, 1999-2014)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you never give up, earn the recognition of others through effort and loyalty, and break cycles of hatred by understanding and forgiving even your enemies.

frames.aligns: Love of enemies and redemption of villains (Gaara, Nagato, Obito); an outcast child's dignity; self-gift for friends; revenge shown as a trap.
frames.concerns: Voyeurism treated as a lovable quirk (Jiraiya); spirit summoning and reanimation, judged by framing; suicide in backstories (Sakumo).

frames.aligns: Forgiveness of enemies and repentance of villains echo theosis; self-sacrifice for friends.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real, so a demon fox sealed in a child, spirit summoning, reanimated dead and a death-god cult read as more than fantasy for many families. Constant killing, which the tradition holds calls for repentance even in war; guarding the senses (nepsis).

frames.aligns: Perseverance, loyalty, a hero who refuses revenge (Romans 12:19). Grace-like acceptance of an outcast (Beneath the Tangles reads Iruka's acceptance through Ephesians 2).
frames.concerns: Spells, summoning and spirits (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); a peeping mentor shown as wise; Tsunade's drinking played for laughs, a concern for teetotal Baptists.

frames.aligns: Servant leadership, grace before merit, forgiveness of enemies (Beneath the Tangles). Many evangelicals accept Tolkien/Lewis-style fantasy magic.
frames.concerns: Chakra, summoning and reanimating the dead may read as spirit contact rather than Tolkien-style magic. Fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, and a hero who will not take revenge.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a demon-like beast sealed in a child, the Jashin blood ritual, spirit summoning and reanimation are often a strong concern even in fiction. Sexual gags and alcohol.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian work shows real goods such as sacrifice and forgiveness. Every main character is flawed, which fits total depravity; villains are not simply monsters.
frames.concerns: Occult imagery; a lascivious mentor (WLC Q139); Sakumo's suicide (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: Naruto cannot earn acceptance by effort alone; it comes first from Iruka. Two kingdoms: rulers bear a sword and can abuse it (Danzo).
frames.concerns: Occult elements (usually adiaphora in fiction, with care); comic nudity.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace: an outcast is loved before he changes. Social holiness: clan discrimination and secret violence challenged. Strong peace theme.
frames.concerns: Tsunade's drinking (holiness churches ask members to abstain); comic nudity.

frames.aligns: Deep roots in fantasy literature (C.S. Lewis); forgiveness, sacrifice, reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Comic nudity; occult-flavored powers, judged by framing.

frames.aligns: The central claim, that revenge must end and enemies be understood, is close to nonresistance.
frames.concerns: Yet nearly every conflict is settled by combat, and fighting is heroic. Conservative groups avoid much fantasy media and value separation from "the world."

frames.aligns: Family and sacrifice; forgiveness; respect for teachers; the ending's marriages and children.
frames.concerns: A peeping mentor shown as wise; alcohol played for laughs (Word of Wisdom); spirit contact.

Reanimated dead and spirits of the dead shown as real conflict with the teaching that the dead sleep (Fundamental Belief 26); drinking; Ellen White's caution about fiction. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Ending the cycle of war; mercy to enemies.
frames.concerns: Spiritism (summoning, reanimation, a death-god cult) is a major concern in jw.org counsel; violence as the main action (Psalm 11:5); loyalty to a military village. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love and understanding overcoming hatred; an outcast's true worth seen.
frames.concerns: Fear, death and despair as recurring mental imagery; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Social justice: criticism of war, clan discrimination, secret police and child soldiers; reconciliation with enemies.
frames.concerns: Gender roles (women as healers and wives); the Killer Bee stereotype CSM flags; fat jokes; harassment humor (Jiraiya).

frames.aligns: Respect for teachers and parents (Exodus 20:12); breaking cycles of revenge (Leviticus 19:18).
frames.concerns: Sorcery and spirit summoning (Deuteronomy 18); mocking speech (fat jokes) as lashon hara-like; nudity gags against tzniut. Haredi homes would avoid it; Modern Orthodox families are selective. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for life and teachers; the end of revenge.
frames.concerns: Spirit summoning; nudity gags; mocking speech. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in the anti-war theme; empathy for the outsider.
frames.concerns: Stereotypes (Killer Bee); gender roles. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Mercy, patience (sabr), care for orphans (Qur'an 93:9), keeping promises, forgiveness over revenge (42:40).
frames.concerns: Alcohol and gambling played for laughs (5:90); sihr and spirit summoning (2:102); Shinto deity names, which some read as shirk imagery. Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes the nudity gags a strong depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like chains of cause and effect, rebirth (Indra and Ashura), chakra as life energy, dharma as duty to community.
frames.concerns: Hindu names (Indra, asura, chakra) used loosely in a fighting story; some may see careless use of sacred terms.

frames.aligns: The "cycle of hatred" mirrors the teaching that hatred is not ended by hatred. Pain's six bodies are named for the six realms. Naruto's choice not to take revenge.
frames.concerns: Buddhist terms used as names of weapons and a villain's bodies; violence (first precept); intoxicants played for laughs (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Kami names, harmony of the village and reverence for ancestors (the stone faces of past Hokage).
frames.concerns: Kami names (Amaterasu, Susanoo, Tsukuyomi, Izanagi) used as weapon names, which some may see as careless; death and blood without purification. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Overcoming ego (haumai) and anger; forgiveness over revenge; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Lust played as comedy (Jiraiya); drinking and gambling. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Unity of nations and the end of war; overcoming prejudice between clans; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Degrading humor against a "chaste and holy life"; drinking and gambling (both forbidden); summoning. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Basically good beings capable of change; survival of the group; honoring teachers and parents.
frames.concerns: Orochimaru's human experiments shown as evil (fits); violence; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Nature energy (Sage Mode); bonds with animal spirits; harm ended through understanding.
frames.concerns: Constant fighting against "harm none"; Hidan's cult as the only explicit religion is a villain's. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: An outcast's dignity, empathy for enemies, criticism of war, secret police and clan discrimination.
frames.concerns: CSM flags sexism, fatphobia, disability clichés and the Killer Bee stereotype. Child soldiers as normal. Women end as wives and mothers (ch. 699-700). Harassment humor.

frames.aligns: Peace comes from people understanding each other, with no god intervening; reason and empathy defeat ideology (Pain, Madara).
frames.concerns: Destiny and bloodline (the reincarnation reveal) cut against self-made achievement.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty to community, respect for teachers and elders, courage, inherited "Will of Fire," marriage and children at the end.
frames.concerns: A "pervert" mentor shown as wise; drinking and gambling; a hero who defies superiors.

frames.aligns: An outcast who becomes his own master; secret authority (Danzo) exposed.
frames.concerns: The story's central rejection of revenge cuts against Church of Satan teaching on retaliation; The Satanic Temple's compassion tenets fit better. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of an outcast; justice and peace; understanding across difference.
frames.concerns: Stereotypes and gender roles CSM flags. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The cycle of revenge is the central problem; Naruto refuses revenge on Pain (ch. 443-453) and refuses to kill Sasuke (ch. 694-699). Winning recognition through effort and keeping one's word are still honored.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Loyalty to the village, respect for teachers and sacrifice for the community are presented as right (Socio-cultural lens). Secret authoritarian rule is critiqued (Danzo, ch. 481; the Uchiha massacre order, ch. 224-225).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The village comes before the clan: the Uchiha coup is the tragedy Itachi stops (vol. 43). Bloodlines still carry inherited powers, and the ending settles the cast into families (ch. 700).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Becoming Hokage is the dream (ch. 700); teachers and the Hokage line are honored, and ninja ranks structure life. Hidden heritage and bloodline decide much of the outcome (Pragmatic lens).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Shinto deity names and Buddhist ideas (the Sage of Six Paths, ch. 671; reincarnated souls) shape the world, though no one prays. The ending shifts toward destiny and myth (Shifts).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: War and sacrifice for the village dominate Part II. Naruto's drive to be acknowledged, and the peace he wins, give some place to self-expression.

folkways.japan: Group loyalty, respect for teachers (sensei and senpai-kohai bonds), duty to the village and the conservative gender roles of the ending reflect postwar Japanese norms; Kishimoto's "war is never the right answer," credited to his grandfather, reflects Japan's postwar pacifism.

delivery.evidence: Fans coined "Talk no Jutsu" for Naruto ending fights with speeches; TV Tropes calls the Pain arc ending a "Writer Cop Out."
delivery.note: Rival theories of peace are argued in speeches during fights and are usually resolved through Naruto's persuasion.

personified.ideology: Peace through shared pain and terror
A few must do terrible things for the many

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (village and "Will of Fire"), Dharmic (Buddhist cycle of hatred), Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics. Lens labels are this entry's framing unless a source is named. Wikipedia's Naruto article notes Confucian values (respect for teachers, filial duty, group over self); the other labels are this entry's own.
